blocks.html: This course looks at Egyptian religion, art and buildings as history: what Egyptians believed and did, as their own texts and monuments show it. If you took the Young Explorers course, you met some of the gods in Many Gods. Here we look more closely at how Egyptians thought about them.

Egyptians worshiped a great many gods. Some were known all over the country, like the sun god Ra or Osiris, the ruler of the dead. Others belonged to one town, one family or one task. The ordinary word for a god was nṯr (said "netjer"). It was written with a sign showing a cloth wound on a pole, the flag that stood in front of every temple.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The word nṯr, "god": the flag on a pole is a word sign; the seated god after it is a determinative, a silent sign that shows the meaning.

blocks.html: One god could appear in several forms, and several gods could share one role. The forms were ways of showing what a god was like, not separate beings.

Thoth, the god of writing, could be an ibis, a man with an ibis head, or a baboon. Hathor could be a cow or a woman wearing cow horns. The sun god had a form for each part of the day in one common scheme: Khepri, the scarab, at sunrise; Ra at noon; Atum, an old man, at evening. Egyptians did not see these as contradictions. Each form showed one side of a power too great for a single picture.
The reverse was also true. Several gods could do the same job. Ra, Atum, Khepri and Horus were all linked with the sun. Many gods and goddesses protected the king or the dead.

Why give a god an animal head? An animal showed a quality people could see. A falcon flies high and sees far, which suits a sky god. A jackal prowls around desert cemeteries, which suits the guardian of the dead. A lioness is fierce, which suits a goddess of war. Putting the head on a human body said: this god acts like a person and has the nature of this animal.

A few chosen animals were believed to house a god’s presence. The Apis bull at Memphis was linked with the god Ptah; when it died, it was buried with great honor in the Serapeum at Saqqara, and a new bull with the right markings was found. In the Late Period, visitors bought millions of mummified ibises, cats and falcons and gave them to gods as lasting offerings.

blocks.title: One god or three?
blocks.q: A temple wall shows an ibis-headed man writing, a statue in the same temple shows a seated baboon, and both are labeled Thoth. Are these three gods?
steps: Look at the labels: both say Thoth.
Thoth’s forms included the ibis, the ibis-headed man and the baboon.
Different forms of one god were normal in Egypt.
blocks.a: One god, Thoth, shown in different forms.

blocks.title: Reading an animal form
blocks.q: Why is Anubis, the god who guards cemeteries, shown with a jackal’s head?
steps: Jackals were seen around the desert edge, where cemeteries were.
The animal head shows the god’s nature and his place.
It is a sign, not a claim that the god was an ordinary jackal.
blocks.a: The jackal suits his role as guardian of the dead.

blocks.html: Saying that Egyptians "worshiped animals". They did not pray to every cat or crocodile. Animal heads and forms showed a god’s qualities, and only a few chosen animals, like the Apis bull, were believed to house a god. Quick check: ask what quality the animal shows.

blocks.html: In Many Gods, Many Forms you saw that one god could have several forms. To read a temple scene, you need to tell the gods apart. The animal head is only the first clue, and often not enough.
Look past the head to the crown, the emblem and the label. Two gods may share a head, but their crowns and emblems differ, and the hieroglyphs beside them name them.

Egyptian artists worked with a shared set of signs. Each god had a crown or an emblem that was part of the god’s name or story: Isis wears a throne because her name is written with the throne sign; Maat wears the feather that writes her name. Learning these emblems is learning a picture language.

blocks.title: Two falcons
blocks.q: A figure has a falcon’s head with a red sun disk circled by a cobra. Who is it?
steps: Falcon head: Ra or Horus (or a combined form).
The sun disk on the head points to Ra; Horus usually wears the double crown.
Check the label to be sure.
blocks.a: Ra (or Ra-Horakhty, the combined sun god).

blocks.title: Two goddesses with horns
blocks.q: A New Kingdom painting shows a woman with cow horns and a sun disk beside Osiris. Is she Hathor?
steps: Cow horns and a sun disk are Hathor’s crown.
But from the New Kingdom on, Isis also wears it.
Beside Osiris, her husband, Isis is the likely choice; the label will say for sure.
blocks.a: Probably Isis; read the name to be certain.

blocks.html: Identifying gods only by the animal head. Ra and Horus are both falcons; Isis and Hathor share a crown in later art; Amun can appear as a ram, like Khnum. Quick check: name the crown or emblem too, and read the label when there is one.

blocks.html: Egypt is a long, narrow river valley with a broad Delta at its northern end, as you saw in The Nile Valley and the Delta. Each town along the river had its own temple and its own gods. A god who was great in one city could be minor in the next.
Each great god had a home city: Ptah at Memphis, Ra at Heliopolis, Amun at Thebes, Thoth at Hermopolis, Osiris at Abydos, Hathor at Dendera.

blocks.html: Why did a god’s fame depend on a city? Temples owned land, workshops and staff, and they grew rich when kings favored them. When a city became the capital, its god rose with it. Memphis was the capital of the Old Kingdom, and Ptah was honored across the land. When Theban kings ruled in the Middle and New Kingdoms, their god Amun became the greatest god of the state. Gods also spread when people moved: Osiris was worshiped everywhere, but pilgrims went to Abydos, where his tomb was believed to be.

blocks.title: From city to god
blocks.q: An inscription says it was set up at Iunu, the city the Greeks called Heliopolis. Which god is its owner most likely praising?
steps: Iunu is Heliopolis, "sun city".
Its gods were Ra and the creator Atum.
So the sun god is the likely subject.
blocks.a: Ra (or Atum, the creator of Heliopolis).

blocks.title: Why Abydos?
blocks.q: Thousands of people who lived far from Abydos set up small stelae there. Why?
steps: Abydos was the cult center of Osiris.
Egyptians believed his burial place was there.
A stela near Osiris let its owner share in his festivals forever.
blocks.a: To be near Osiris, ruler of the dead.

blocks.html: Thinking every god was worshiped equally everywhere. Each city honored its own gods first; the great gods spread when their cities were powerful. Quick check: when you meet a god, ask "which city?"

blocks.html: Many cities grouped their gods as a family, as you saw with the home cities of the gods. Scholars call such a group of three a triad: usually a father, a mother and a child.
Learn the triads with their cities: Amun, Mut and Khonsu at Thebes; Ptah, Sekhmet and Nefertem at Memphis; Khnum, Satet and Anuket at Elephantine; and the royal family of Osiris, Isis and Horus.

blocks.html: Why families? Egyptians understood the world through human life: birth, marriage, parents and heirs. A family of gods gave a city a complete divine household and a story. It also linked gods who had once been separate: a city’s main god could be given a wife and a son from nearby towns. The family of Osiris, Isis and Horus mattered most for kingship, because every king was Horus, the son and heir.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The divine family behind kingship: Osiris, Isis and their son Horus.

blocks.title: Placing a son
blocks.q: A relief at Karnak shows a young god with a side lock of hair and a moon disk. Which family is he in?
steps: The moon disk points to Khonsu, the moon god.
Khonsu is the son in the Theban triad.
Karnak is at Thebes, so this fits.
blocks.a: The Theban triad: Amun, Mut and Khonsu.

blocks.title: Memphis or Thebes?
blocks.q: A statue of a lioness-headed goddess comes from Memphis. Whose wife is she?
steps: A lioness-headed goddess at Memphis is Sekhmet.
Sekhmet is the wife of Ptah.
Their son is Nefertem.
blocks.a: Ptah’s wife, Sekhmet.

blocks.html: Mixing up the triads, for example making Sekhmet the wife of Amun. Tie each family to its city: Thebes has Amun, Mut and Khonsu; Memphis has Ptah, Sekhmet and Nefertem. Quick check: the city gives you the family.
Families were not fixed everywhere. A goddess like Hathor could be paired with different gods in different temples. The triads above are the best-known pairings, not rules for all of Egypt.

The best-known Egyptian myth tells of the family you met in Divine Families: Osiris, his wife Isis, their son Horus, and Osiris’s brother Seth. It explains why the dead could live again and why each king could claim the throne.

items: Osiris ruled Egypt as a good king.
His brother Seth killed him out of jealousy. In some versions he scattered the body.
Isis, helped by her sister Nephthys and by Anubis, searched for Osiris, gathered him and restored him to life long enough to conceive a son.
Isis raised Horus in hiding in the marshes of the Delta.
Grown up, Horus fought Seth. He lost an eye, which was healed. The gods judged in his favor, and Horus became king.
Osiris did not return to rule the living. He became king of the dead.

blocks.html: Four roles to remember: Osiris, the murdered king who rules the dead; Seth, his killer; Isis, who restored him; Horus, the son who won the throne.

The myth matched the life of kingship. The living king was Horus; when he died he became Osiris, and his son became the new Horus. It also gave every person a hope: as Osiris was restored, the dead could be too. The healed eye of Horus, the wedjat ("the sound one"), became an amulet for wholeness.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Osiris, wsjr: the seat writes ws, the eye writes jr, and the seated god is a determinative.

blocks.html: No Egyptian text tells the whole myth from start to finish. The Pyramid Texts, hymns and spells refer to its parts. A New Kingdom papyrus, the Contendings of Horus and Seth, tells the trial between the two gods with much humor. The fullest single telling is in Greek, in the essay On Isis and Osiris by Plutarch, written about AD 100. Plutarch adds details, like a chest in which Seth trapped Osiris, that we cannot always trace in Egyptian sources.

blocks.title: Using the myth
blocks.q: A tomb text calls the dead man "the Osiris Nakht". What does that tell us about Egyptian belief?
steps: Osiris died and was restored, then ruled the dead.
Calling the dead man an Osiris joins him with that hope.
It is a statement of belief about his new life, not his job.
blocks.a: Egyptians hoped each justified dead person would live again, like Osiris.

blocks.title: Weighing a source
blocks.q: A book says, "The Egyptians believed Seth cut Osiris into fourteen pieces." What should you ask?
steps: Where does the number come from?
The number fourteen comes from Plutarch, a Greek writer of about AD 100.
Egyptian sources tell the story in pieces, and the details vary.
blocks.a: It is one version, told late, by a Greek author.

blocks.html: Expecting one fixed, official version of the story. Egyptian texts give pieces, and they differ; the only complete telling is Plutarch’s, much later. Quick check: when you read a detail, ask which source it comes from.

blocks.html: The gods of Egypt’s divine families could also be joined to one another. The most famous joined god is Amun-Ra, the king of the gods in the New Kingdom.

Amun (jmn, "the hidden one") began as a god of Thebes. When Theban kings reunited Egypt in the Middle Kingdom, Amun rose with them; several 12th Dynasty kings were named Amenemhat, "Amun is foremost". In the New Kingdom, joined with the sun god Ra as Amun-Ra, he became the great god of the state, and his temple at Karnak became the richest in Egypt.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Amun, jmn: the reed (j), the game board (mn) with n as a phonetic complement, and the seated god as determinative.

blocks.html: Gods could be joined into one: Amun-Ra joins the hidden god of Thebes with the sun god of Heliopolis. Joining added a form; it did not replace the older gods.

Why join gods? Each god stood for a power. Amun was unseen and everywhere; Ra was the visible sun that gave life. Joined, Amun-Ra was both: hidden and shining, creator and king. Egyptian theologians often said one god "was in" another. Scholars call this syncretism. Other examples are Ra-Horakhty ("Ra, Horus of the Two Horizons"), Sobek-Ra and Ptah-Sokar-Osiris.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Amun’s story on the timeline: his rise with the Theban kings, the high point of the New Kingdom, the break under Akhenaten and the return under Tutankhamun.

blocks.title: Separate or joined?
blocks.q: A New Kingdom hymn praises Amun-Ra at Karnak, and another praises Ra at Heliopolis. Does the second show that Ra was replaced?
steps: Amun-Ra is a joined form.
Ra kept his own cult and temple at Heliopolis.
Both hymns can come from the same years.
blocks.a: No: Ra was still worshiped in his own right.

blocks.title: A break in the story
blocks.q: Why were Amun’s name and images hacked out in many places during the reign of Akhenaten?
steps: Akhenaten put the sun disk, the Aten, above all gods.
He closed the temples of Amun and had his name removed.
Tutankhamun later restored Amun, whose name is part of his own.
blocks.a: Akhenaten’s religious change; it did not last.

blocks.html: Thinking a combined god replaced the older ones. Amun and Ra were still worshiped separately, side by side with Amun-Ra. Quick check: a joined name keeps both names, because both gods are still there.

blocks.html: Egyptians told several stories of how the world began, each tied to a great temple city. The oldest we can trace is the account of Heliopolis (Iunu), the city of the sun god you met in Many Gods, Many Forms. Its pieces appear already in the Pyramid Texts of the late Old Kingdom.

Before anything existed there was Nun: dark, endless, motionless water. From it the creator Atum ("the complete one") came into being by himself, standing on the first land. Atum produced the first pair of gods without a partner; the Pyramid Texts say he sneezed out Shu and spat out Tefnut.

blocks.cap: The Ennead of Heliopolis: 1 + 2 + 2 + 4 = 9 gods.

blocks.html: Atum rose from the waters of Nun and made Shu and Tefnut; they had Geb (earth) and Nut (sky); Geb and Nut had Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys. Together these nine are the Ennead.

The account explains the world by a family tree. First comes the space of air and moisture that life needs; then the ground below and the sky above; then the gods of kingship and death, who connect the cosmos to human life. Shu, the air, stands between Geb and Nut and holds them apart, which is why there is room to live. Scenes show Nut arched over Geb with Shu lifting her up.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Geb, the earth god: the goose writes gb, the foot repeats b, and the seated god is a determinative.

blocks.html: The Greeks called the group the Ennead, from their word for "nine"; the Egyptians said psḏt. The word could also simply mean "all the gods", and some lists add other gods such as Horus.

blocks.title: Following the family tree
blocks.q: In the Heliopolis account, who are the grandparents of Osiris?
steps: Osiris’s parents are Geb and Nut.
Geb and Nut are the children of Shu and Tefnut.
So Shu and Tefnut are his grandparents.
blocks.a: Shu and Tefnut.

blocks.title: Counting the Nine
blocks.q: How many gods are in the Ennead, and how do you check?
steps: Count by generation: Atum (1).
Shu and Tefnut (2), Geb and Nut (2).
Osiris, Isis, Seth and Nephthys (4).
blocks.a: Nine.

blocks.html: Naming Ra as the first god in every account. At Heliopolis the creator is Atum; Ra was joined with him later, and at Memphis the creator is Ptah. Quick check: ask which city the account comes from.

blocks.html: Memphis, the old capital, had its own account of creation, built on the one from Heliopolis. In it the creator is Ptah, the god of Memphis and patron of craftsmen.

Ptah created the world by thought and word: he conceived everything in his heart and brought it into being by speaking with his tongue. The text survives on the Shabaka Stone, carved in the 25th Dynasty; when it was first composed is debated.

In the Memphis account, Atum and the Ennead do not disappear. They come into being through Ptah, and the Ennead are pictured as the teeth and lips in Ptah’s mouth, the organs of his creative speech. The older account is placed inside the newer one.

For Egyptians the heart was the seat of thought and the tongue made thought real. A command from the king made things happen; a name spoken in a ritual called its owner to life. So creation by "heart and tongue" made sense: the world exists because a god thought of it and named it. It also gave Memphis a claim: its god stood before the creator of Heliopolis.

The text is carved on a slab of dark stone now in the British Museum. Its opening says that King Shabaka, a Kushite king of the 25th Dynasty (c. 716–702 BC in Shaw’s dates), found an ancient writing eaten by worms and had it copied on stone. Later the stone was used as a millstone: a square hole in the middle and grinding marks have worn away much of the text.

Early 20th-century scholars, among them Breasted, read the old-fashioned language as proof that the text was Old Kingdom. Since the 1970s many scholars have argued that it was written much later, perhaps in the New Kingdom or in Shabaka’s own time, in a style made to look ancient. There is no agreement, so it is best to say: the stone is 25th Dynasty, and the date of the text is debated.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Ptah, ptḥ: stool (p), loaf (t), twisted flax (ḥ), and the seated god determinative.

blocks.title: Dating carefully
blocks.q: A guidebook says, "The Memphite Theology is the oldest philosophy in the world, from c. 2500 BC." How should you correct it?
steps: The stone itself dates from Shabaka’s reign, c. 716–702 BC.
Its language looks old, but many scholars think it was written later in an old style.
The date of composition is debated.
blocks.a: Say: the stone is 25th Dynasty; when the text was written is debated.

blocks.title: Two creators
blocks.q: How can Atum be the creator at Heliopolis and Ptah the creator at Memphis?
steps: Each city told the story with its own god first.
The Memphis text includes Atum and the Ennead, as Ptah’s mouth.
Egyptians held such accounts side by side.
blocks.a: Memphis placed the Heliopolis account inside its own.

blocks.html: Dating the Memphite Theology to the Old Kingdom as a fact. The stone is from the 25th Dynasty, and scholars disagree about how much older the text is. Quick check: keep the date of the object and the date of the text apart.

sources.name: James Henry Breasted, "The Philosophy of a Memphite Priest" (1901), for the early view of its date

blocks.html: A third account belongs to Hermopolis in Middle Egypt, the city of Thoth (see Gods and Their Cities). It does not begin with one creator, as at Heliopolis, but with eight gods who stood for the waters before creation.

At Hermopolis, creation began with the Ogdoad, "the Eight": four pairs of gods and goddesses standing for the waters, endlessness, darkness and hiddenness. Ogdoad (eight, Hermopolis) is not the Ennead (nine, Heliopolis).

Goddess
Stands for
blocks.cap: The four pairs of the Ogdoad. The goddesses’ names are the gods’ names with a feminine ending.

blocks.html: The eight do not describe a world but the state before one: water with no edge, no light and nothing that can be seen. By naming these as gods, the account made the chaos itself the starting point of creation. Pairing each quality as male and female made it able to produce something new. The gods were often shown with frogs’ heads and the goddesses with snakes’ heads, creatures of the mud and water.

The city’s Egyptian name was Khemenu, "Eight Town", after these gods. The Greeks matched Thoth with their god Hermes, and so called it Hermopolis. In some versions the eight brought forth a lotus flower on the waters, from which the sun rose; in others, a cosmic egg.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Hermopolis in Middle Egypt, between Memphis and Thebes. Tap it for its note.

blocks.title: Ogdoad or Ennead?
blocks.q: A text speaks of "the Eight who were in Nun". Which account is it drawing on?
steps: "Eight" is the Ogdoad.
The Ogdoad belongs to Hermopolis.
The Ennead of Heliopolis has nine.
blocks.a: The Hermopolis account.

blocks.title: A god in two places
blocks.q: Amun is in the Ogdoad. Why did that matter to the priests of Thebes?
steps: Amun stands for hiddenness in the Ogdoad.
Amun was the great god of Thebes.
Theban priests could say the Eight were Amun’s, making their god part of the first moment.
blocks.a: It let Thebes claim Amun was present at creation.

blocks.html: Confusing the Ogdoad (eight gods, Hermopolis) with the Ennead (nine gods, Heliopolis). Quick check: Hermopolis’s own name, Khemenu, means "Eight Town", so the Eight belong there.

blocks.html: You have now met three creation accounts: Heliopolis, Memphis and Hermopolis. They name different first gods, but they share a picture.

All the accounts begin with the waters of Nun and a first mound of land rising from them. The benben stone, the tips of pyramids and obelisks, and the raised floor of the temple sanctuary all recall that mound.

Egyptians watched the picture happen every year. When the Nile flood went down in autumn, mounds of fresh, dark land rose out of the water, and soon plants grew on them. Creation looked like that: life rising from water. A mound was the first firm place to stand, and the place where the sun first rose.

items: At Heliopolis the benben, a pointed stone, stood for the first mound on which the sun first shone. Its name is linked to the word wbn, "to rise, shine".
The pointed capstone of a pyramid and the tip of an obelisk (the pyramidion) echo the benben.
At Memphis the risen land was the god Tatenen, joined with Ptah as Ptah-Tatenen.
In temples the floor rises toward the sanctuary, the god’s room, which stands for the mound.

blocks.name: eg-temple
blocks.cap: The plan and side view of a temple: the floor rises and the roof drops toward the sanctuary, the place of the first mound.

blocks.html: Egyptians did not see the accounts as rivals that cancel each other. Each showed a side of the same mystery, and later texts combine them freely: Atum can stand on the mound, Ptah can be that mound, and the Eight can be in the waters around it.

blocks.title: Reading a monument
blocks.q: Why might an obelisk’s tip have been covered with gold or electrum?
steps: The tip echoes the benben, where the sun first shone.
A shining metal tip would catch the first rays of sunrise.
So the tip recalls the first sunrise on the first mound.
blocks.a: To catch the sun, like the benben at creation.

blocks.title: One picture, three stories
blocks.q: What do the Heliopolis and Hermopolis accounts share, though their gods differ?
steps: Both begin with the waters of Nun.
In both, something rises from the waters: Atum on the mound, or a lotus with the sun.
Both mark the first appearance of the sun.
blocks.a: Waters, a rising, and the first sunrise.

blocks.html: Treating the accounts as competing claims, where only one can be right. Egyptians held several side by side and mixed them. Quick check: look for the shared picture, the mound in the waters.

blocks.html: In Many Gods, Many Forms you met gods who stand for powers of nature. Maat stands for something different: the way the world ought to be.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The word mꜣꜥt, "Maat": the pedestal writes mꜣꜥ, the forearm repeats ꜥ, the loaf is the feminine ending, and the papyrus roll marks an abstract idea.

blocks.html: Maat (mꜣꜥt) was the right order of the world: truth, justice and balance. Its opposite was isfet (jzft), disorder and wrongdoing. Keeping maat was the duty of gods, kings and ordinary people.

Egyptians lived by a river that could flood too much or too little, beside deserts full of danger. Order was not automatic; it had to be kept up. The sun had to rise, the flood had to come, the weak had to be protected from the strong. Maat named that whole order, in the sky and in society alike. When people were honest, fair and generous, they were doing maat; when they cheated or did violence, they fed isfet.

blocks.text: Maat as a goddess and an idea

blocks.html: As a goddess, Maat is a woman with an ostrich feather on her head, daughter of the sun god. The same feather sits on the scale when the hearts of the dead are weighed. As an idea, maat runs through every part of life:

items: The king’s first task was to "put maat in place of isfet". On temple walls he offers the gods a small figure of Maat, the gift that sums up all others.
Judges and viziers held titles like "priest of Maat"; justice was doing maat.
Wisdom texts, like the Instruction of Ptahhotep, teach that maat lasts while wrongdoing fails in the end.
In the story of the Eloquent Peasant, a robbed farmer asks an official again and again to do maat for him.

blocks.title: Maat or isfet?
blocks.q: A tomb owner writes: "I gave bread to the hungry and clothes to the naked; I did not move a boundary stone." What is he claiming?
steps: Feeding and clothing the poor is doing maat.
Moving a boundary stone steals land, an act of isfet.
He says he kept maat and avoided isfet.
blocks.a: He claims to have lived by maat.

blocks.title: Reading an offering scene
blocks.q: A relief shows the king holding up a seated goddess with a feather toward Amun. What is happening?
steps: The seated goddess with a feather is Maat.
The king is offering Maat to the god.
He shows that he has kept order, which is what the gods want most.
blocks.a: The offering of Maat.

blocks.html: Thinking Maat is only a goddess. Maat is also an idea, the order everyone was to live by. Quick check: if a text says someone "did maat", read it as "did what is right".

blocks.html: The history course described the king’s government in Divine Kingship and the Titulary. Here we look at the religious side: what Egyptians believed the king was. It builds on Maat and Isfet, because keeping maat was the king’s first duty.
The king was Horus on earth and the son of Ra. He stood between the gods and the people, offering to the gods on behalf of everyone. The office was divine; the man who held it was mortal.
From the Middle Kingdom on, a king had five names, his titulary. Each told something about his nature:

head: Name
Introduced by
What it says
rows: a falcon on a palace facade
the king is the living Horus
the vulture and the cobra goddesses
protected by the goddesses of Upper and Lower Egypt
a falcon on the sign for gold
nsw-bjt, "King of Upper and Lower Egypt"
the name taken at the coronation
blocks.cap: The five-part royal titulary. Only the last two are written in cartouches.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs

opts.en: King of Upper and Lower Egypt, son of Ra

blocks.cap: The two titles that introduce the cartouches: nsw-bjt and zꜣ-rꜥ.

blocks.html: Why make the king divine? Egypt needed one person who could speak to every god, keep maat and hold the Two Lands together. The myth of Osiris gave the model: the living king is Horus, son of Osiris, and when he dies he becomes Osiris. But the man was human. Kings aged and died, fought wars they could lose, and could be plotted against: papyri record the trial of people who conspired against Ramesses III. The divinity belonged to the office, which passed from king to king, more than to the person.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: The birth name of Ramesses II, rꜥ-ms-sw, "Ra is the one who bore him", inside its cartouche.

blocks.title: Reading the titles
blocks.q: A cartouche follows the title zꜣ-rꜥ. Which of the king’s names is it?
steps: zꜣ-rꜥ means "son of Ra".
It introduces the birth name.
nsw-bjt would introduce the throne name.
blocks.a: The birth name.

blocks.title: God or man?
blocks.q: Was a king like Ramesses II a god to his people?
steps: As holder of the office, he was Horus and son of Ra.
As a man, he grew old and died after about 66 years of rule.
Egyptians kept both ideas at once.
blocks.a: The office was divine; the man was mortal.

blocks.html: Saying that Egyptians saw the king simply as a god. The office was divine, but the man holding it could fall ill, be criticized in literature or be the target of a plot. Quick check: separate what the titles claim from what the records show.

blocks.html: As The King Between Gods and People explained, the king stood between the gods and the people. Temple walls make that idea visible: in scene after scene, the king faces a god and gives a gift.
Temple scenes show the king offering to the gods in every scene. In practice, priests performed the daily rites in his name, as his deputies.

In theory the king was the one priest of every god in Egypt. That could not work in practice: there were hundreds of temples and only one king. So priests acted on his behalf. The scenes on the walls showed the ideal, which Egyptians believed was also true in a deeper way: through the king, Egypt served the gods, and the gods gave life to Egypt. Carved in stone, the king’s offering would go on forever.

blocks.text: What the king offers, and what he gets back

head: The king gives
The god gives in return
blocks.cap: Captions beside offering scenes record the gifts on both sides.

blocks.name: eg-temple
blocks.cap: A temple from the river to the sanctuary. Offering scenes cover its walls; the deepest rooms show the most sacred rites.

blocks.html: The same idea reached private tombs. The offering formula on tombs and stelae begins ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives". Even when a family brought bread to a tomb, the gift was, in words, the king’s.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives". The word for king is written first out of honor but read last.

blocks.title: Who really did it?
blocks.q: A wall of the Ptolemaic temple at Edfu shows the king pouring water for Horus. Did the king travel to Edfu to do this every day?
steps: The scene shows the ideal: the king serves the god.
Daily rites were performed by Edfu’s priests in his name.
The carving makes his service permanent.
blocks.a: No; priests acted for him.

blocks.title: Reading a private stela
blocks.q: Why does an ordinary official’s stela begin "an offering that the king gives to Osiris"?
steps: Offerings flowed, in theory, through the king.
The formula names the king as the giver.
It then asks for bread, beer and other goods for the official.
blocks.a: Because every offering was given, in words, through the king.

blocks.html: Thinking the king performed every ritual in person. Priests acted on his behalf; the scenes show what the king’s office meant. Quick check: count the temples, and remember there was one king.

blocks.html: A king who had ruled for many years could renew his strength in a great festival, the sed (ḥb-sd), often called the jubilee. It builds on The King Between Gods and People: the king’s power had to be renewed for Egypt to stay in order.
The sed festival renewed the king’s strength and his right to rule. It was traditionally held first after thirty years of rule and then every few years after that.

A king’s power was tied to his body. An old and weak king could seem to put maat at risk. The sed was a way to renew him without a new king: rites repeated parts of the coronation, the king ran a ritual course to show his vigor and claim the land again, and gods from all over Egypt were brought to confirm him.

items: Djoser’s Step Pyramid complex (3rd Dynasty) has a court for the festival, lined with rows of dummy chapels. Djoser reigned less than thirty years; the court gave him a sed that would last forever in the afterlife.
Reliefs show the king running between boundary markers.
Amenhotep III celebrated three sed festivals, in his 30th, 34th and 37th years.
Ramesses II, who ruled about 66 years, held about thirteen or fourteen.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Three kings linked with the sed: Djoser (whose complex has a sed court), Amenhotep III and Ramesses II.

blocks.title: Counting the years
blocks.q: A king held his first sed festival in year 30 and then one every 3 years. In which year was his third festival?
steps: Festival 1: year 30.
Festival 2: 30 + 3 = 33.
Festival 3: 33 + 3 = 36.
blocks.a: Year 36.

blocks.title: Long enough?
blocks.q: Using the reign dates, could Tutankhamun (c. 1336–1327 BC) have reached the traditional time for a first sed festival?
steps: His reign lasted about 1336 − 1327 = 9 years.
The tradition put the first sed in year 30.
Nine years is far short of thirty.
blocks.a: No.

blocks.html: Calling the sed festival a birthday party. It was a jubilee of renewal, counted from the start of the reign, not from the king’s birth, and usually first held in the 30th year. Quick check: count years of rule, not years of age.
Thirty years was a tradition, not a fixed rule. A few kings held a sed earlier, and scholars still discuss why.

blocks.html: In The King Offers to the Gods you saw the king serving the gods on temple walls. Now we look at the temples themselves. Egyptians built two main kinds, and telling them apart helps you read any site.
A cult temple was the house of a god, where the god’s statue lived and was cared for. A memorial (mortuary) temple kept up the cult of a dead king, joined with a god, forever.

head: Cult temple
Memorial temple
rows: Karnak and Luxor (Amun), Edfu (Horus), Dendera (Hathor), Philae (Isis)
Deir el-Bahari (Hatshepsut), the Ramesseum (Ramesses II), Medinet Habu (Ramesses III)
east bank, with the living city
blocks.cap: The two main kinds of temple.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Thebes: the cult temples of Karnak and Luxor on the east bank; the memorial temples, the Valleys of the Kings and Queens and the workmen’s village on the west bank.

blocks.html: Why put the memorial temples on the west bank? The sun sets in the west, and Egyptians placed the land of the dead there. In the New Kingdom, kings hid their tombs in the Valley of the Kings and built their memorial temples at the edge of the fields, where priests could bring offerings every day. The cult temples of the living gods stood on the east bank, with the city.

Neither kind was a place for public worship like a church or a mosque. A temple was a god’s house, closed to most people. Ordinary Egyptians could come into the outer courts on feast days, pray at the gates, and see the god when the statue came out in procession.

blocks.title: Which kind?
blocks.q: Medinet Habu stands on the west bank at Thebes, and its walls celebrate the victories of Ramesses III. What kind of temple is it?
steps: West bank at Thebes: the side of the dead.
It celebrates a king and kept his cult.
So it is a memorial temple.
blocks.a: The memorial temple of Ramesses III.

blocks.title: Reading a name
blocks.q: The temple at Dendera is dedicated to Hathor and was finished in Roman times. What kind is it?
steps: It houses a goddess, Hathor.
It is not tied to one dead king.
So it is a cult temple.
blocks.a: A cult temple of Hathor.

blocks.html: Thinking temples were for public worship, like churches. Most people never went inside; temples were the houses of the gods, served by priests. Quick check: ask who lived there, a god, or the cult of a king.
Some temples were cut into rock instead of built. At Abu Simbel in Nubia, Ramesses II cut two temples into a cliff; they were moved to higher ground in 1964–68 when Lake Nasser rose.

blocks.html: Most New Kingdom and later temples follow one plan, as the two kinds of temple both show. Walking in from the river, you pass a set of parts in a fixed order.

blocks.name: eg-temple
blocks.cap: The temple plan, numbered from the river: 1 quay, 2 avenue of sphinxes, 3 pylon, 4 open court, 5 hypostyle hall, 6 offering hall, 7 sanctuary. The side view shows the floor rising and the roof dropping.

blocks.html: From the river: quay, avenue of sphinxes, pylon, open court, hypostyle hall, offering hall, sanctuary.

head: Part
What it is
rows: a landing on the river or a canal for the god’s boat at festivals
a processional way lined with sphinxes
the great gateway: two towers with a door between, with flagpoles and often a pair of obelisks
a courtyard open to the sky, often with columns along the sides
a roofed hall full of columns, lit by high windows
a smaller hall where offerings were laid out
the god’s room, with the shrine (naos) for the statue
blocks.cap: Around them: an enclosure wall of mud brick and a sacred lake for purification.

blocks.html: The order follows a single idea: each step takes you further from the outside world and closer to the god. The doorways get smaller, the rooms darker, the people allowed in fewer. Crowds might reach the court on a feast day; the hypostyle hall was for priests; the sanctuary for the king and the high priests. You will see in The Temple as the World that the order also pictures the world.

blocks.title: Step by step
blocks.q: You have just passed through the pylon. What comes next?
steps: The pylon is the gateway.
Behind it is the open court.
After the court comes the hypostyle hall.
blocks.a: The open court.

blocks.title: Reading a real temple
blocks.q: Karnak has six pylons one behind another along its main axis. Does that break the plan?
steps: The plan is a pattern: gateway, court, hall, sanctuary.
Each king who enlarged Karnak added a new gateway and court in front of the old ones.
So a big temple repeats parts of the plan, but the order from the river inward stays the same.
blocks.a: No: Karnak repeats the parts, in the same order.

blocks.html: Putting the hypostyle hall before the pylon. The pylon is the gateway; everything else lies behind it. Quick check: you cannot enter a hall before you pass through the gate.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Ancient Egyptian temple" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: You learned the parts in The Plan of a Temple and the first mound in The First Mound. Put the two together and the temple becomes a picture of the world at the moment of creation.

The temple pictured the world at creation: the pylon was the horizon, the columns a papyrus marsh, the ceiling the sky, and the sanctuary the first mound. The floor rises and the light dims toward the sanctuary.

head: Part
What it stood for
rows: the horizon: its two towers are like two hills with the sun rising between them
a papyrus marsh at the edge of the first waters: columns shaped as stems, capitals as flowers or buds
the sky, painted blue with yellow stars or flying vultures
the earth and the river, with plants and offering-bearers
the first mound, on the highest floor, in darkness
blocks.cap: The temple as a model of the world.

blocks.name: eg-temple
blocks.cap: The side view: as you walk in, the floor climbs and the roof comes down toward the sanctuary.

blocks.html: A temple was where creation was renewed every day. By making the building a model of the first moment, Egyptians made each morning’s ritual a new beginning. The pylon’s shape echoed the hieroglyph for "horizon", the place where the sun appears. Walking inward took you from the bright world of people into the dark, rising ground of the first mound, where the god lived.

blocks.title: Why rise?
blocks.q: A visitor notices the floor slopes upward through the halls. What did that mean to the builders?
steps: The sanctuary stood for the first mound.
A mound is high ground rising from water.
So the floor climbs toward it.
blocks.a: The climb toward the first mound of creation.

blocks.title: Reading the columns
blocks.q: Why are the columns of a hypostyle hall carved like bundles of papyrus?
steps: Papyrus grew in marshes at the water’s edge.
The hall stood for the marsh around the first mound.
So the columns are plants in stone.
blocks.a: They make the hall a marsh at the edge of the first waters.

blocks.html: Seeing the plan only as a series of rooms. Each part carried meaning, which is why floors rise and roofs drop toward the sanctuary. Quick check: for any part, ask "what does it stand for?"

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Ancient Egyptian temple" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: A temple was a god’s house, as The Plan of a Temple showed, and the god was looked after like an honored guest. Every morning, at dawn, priests performed the main daily ritual in the sanctuary.
Each morning priests opened the shrine, woke, washed, dressed and fed the god’s statue, then sealed it again. Egyptians believed the god came to dwell in the statue.

blocks.text: The morning ritual, step by step

items: The priests purified themselves, washing in the sacred lake.
The officiating priest broke the clay seal on the shrine and opened its doors, "revealing the face" of the god.
He burned incense and sang a hymn to wake the god.
He cleaned the statue, anointed it with oil, dressed it in fresh linen and put on its ornaments.
He laid out food and drink before it.
He backed out of the room, sweeping away his footprints, and sealed the doors again.

blocks.html: Why care for a statue as if it were alive? Egyptians believed the god’s presence came to rest in its image, as a person lives in a body. A neglected god might leave, and with the god would go the order of the world. So the ritual kept the god present and content, every day. Shorter rites followed at midday and in the evening.

The food was not wasted. After the god had received it, it "reverted" to the priests and temple staff, who ate it. Scenes of the daily ritual survive in the chapels of the temple of Seti I at Abydos, and papyri preserve the words the priests said.

blocks.name: eg-temple
blocks.cap: The ritual took place in the sanctuary (7), the deepest room. Priests purified themselves at the sacred lake first.

blocks.title: Putting the steps in order
blocks.q: Order these: dress the statue, purify, seal the shrine, open the shrine.
steps: Purity comes first, before entering.
The shrine must be opened before the statue can be cared for.
Dressing comes before the shrine is sealed again.
blocks.a: Purify, open the shrine, dress the statue, seal the shrine.

blocks.title: Where did the bread go?
blocks.q: A temple received hundreds of loaves a day for the god. What happened to them?
steps: They were offered to the god first.
Then they reverted to the temple’s people.
Offerings paid and fed the priests and staff.
blocks.a: The priests and staff ate them after the god had received them.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians believed the statue was the god. They believed the god came to dwell in it. Quick check: the same god could dwell in statues in many temples at once.

Wikipedia, "Temple of Seti I (Abydos)" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: The The Daily Ritual needed people to perform it. Egyptian priests were organized by rank and by shift.

head: Title
Meaning
Role
rows: senior priests; the "first god’s servant" was the high priest
ordinary priests who carried the god’s boat and handled offerings
the one who carries the ritual book
the lector priest, who read the texts aloud
women singers in the god’s choir
blocks.cap: Some common titles. Their words for "god" and "pure" appear in many other titles.

blocks.html: Priests served in shifts: temple staff were divided into four groups (phyles) that took turns, one month each, so many priests served one month in four and then went back to their own lives.

Why shifts? A temple needed people every day, but most priests were also farmers, scribes or officials, with land and families. Rotating groups let many people share the work and the income from the temple’s offerings. While on duty a priest had to be pure: he shaved his body, washed several times a day, wore linen and kept rules about food. The Greek historian Herodotus noticed the shaving and the linen.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nṯr, "god", the second half of the title ḥm-nṯr, "god’s servant".

blocks.html: At the top of a great temple stood the high priest. The First God’s Servant of Amun at Karnak ran the richest temple in Egypt, with huge estates. Women served as chantresses, and a royal woman held the office of God’s Wife of Amun at Thebes.

blocks.title: Months on duty
blocks.q: Staff were in four groups that served one month each in turn. How many months a year did one priest serve?
steps: Twelve months shared by four groups.
Each priest served one month in four.
blocks.a: 3 months a year.

blocks.title: Reading a title
blocks.q: A stela calls its owner "lector priest". What did he do?
steps: The lector carried the ritual book.
He read the sacred texts aloud in rituals.
Lector priests also read at funerals.
blocks.a: He recited the rituals from the papyrus.

blocks.html: Picturing priests as full-time monks who never left the temple. Many served one month in four and spent the rest of the year in their ordinary lives. Quick check: four phyles means three months a year on duty.

blocks.html: The greatest temple of Egypt was Karnak, the house of Amun-Ra at Thebes. It follows the temple plan, but many times over, because it grew for two thousand years.
Karnak, the temple of Amun at Thebes, grew from the Middle Kingdom to Roman times; an avenue of sphinxes joins it to Luxor Temple, about 3 km to the south.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Karnak and Luxor Temple on the east bank of Thebes, joined by the avenue of sphinxes.

blocks.html: Why did one temple keep growing? Every king wanted to honor Amun, the god who gave him victory, and to leave his name where it would last. Kings added pylons, courts, halls, obelisks and chapels, usually in front of or around what was there, so the oldest parts lie deepest inside. Egyptians called it Ipet-isut, "the most select of places".

head: King
What he added
rows: the White Chapel, a small shrine for the god’s boat
the Great Hypostyle Hall, with 134 columns
more gates and pylons, and the first pylon
blocks.cap: Some of the builders of Karnak, from the oldest.

blocks.html: Luxor Temple, Ipet-resyt, was built mostly by Amenhotep III; Ramesses II added a court, a pylon and a pair of obelisks. One of those obelisks has stood in the Place de la Concorde in Paris since the 1830s. Karnak also held the precincts of Mut, Amun’s wife, to the south and of the war god Montu to the north.

blocks.title: Oldest parts deepest
blocks.q: Thutmose III’s Festival Hall lies at the back of Karnak, behind the sanctuary area; the first pylon is at the front. Which is likely older?
steps: Kings usually added new gates and courts in front.
So the front pylon is likely later.
Indeed, the first pylon was built in the Late Period or later.
blocks.a: The Festival Hall (New Kingdom); the front pylon came last.

blocks.title: Counting columns
blocks.q: The Great Hypostyle Hall has 12 giant columns along its center aisle and 122 smaller ones. How many in all?
blocks.a: 134 columns.

blocks.html: Thinking Karnak was built all at once. Kings from the Middle Kingdom to the Romans added to it. Quick check: names of many kings, from many dynasties, are carved on its walls.

blocks.html: Most of the year the god stayed hidden in the sanctuary, as you saw in The Daily Ritual. At festivals the god came out. The greatest festival of Thebes was Opet, which linked the two temples of Karnak and Luxor.
In the Opet festival, the statue of Amun traveled in its sacred boat from Karnak to Luxor Temple, with Mut and Khonsu, and the king’s divine power was renewed there.

items: Priests lifted Amun’s portable boat-shrine, a small sacred boat (bark) with a cabin hiding the statue, onto their shoulders.
Mut and Khonsu followed in their own boats.

The procession went south to Luxor Temple, on foot along the avenue of sphinxes or on great barges on the river. Early in the 18th Dynasty it went by land and came back by water; later both ways were often by river.
At Luxor the king entered the inner rooms with the god, and his royal ka, the divine power of kingship, was renewed.
After some days, the gods returned to Karnak.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The route of Opet: from Karnak south to Luxor Temple, about 3 km, by the avenue of sphinxes or the river.

blocks.html: Why travel? A festival let the god act in the world. The visit to Luxor renewed Amun as a creator and renewed the king as his son, so the whole order of Egypt was refreshed for another year. It also brought the god near the people: crowds lined the route, musicians played, and there was food and drink. People could ask the god questions as the boat passed, a practice you will meet in Oracles and Letters to the Dead.

Opet was held in the second month of Akhet, the flood season. Under Thutmose III it lasted about 11 days; by the 20th Dynasty it ran for more than three weeks. Its procession is carved on the walls of the great colonnade at Luxor Temple, decorated under Tutankhamun and Horemheb.

blocks.title: Which way?
blocks.q: Where did the Opet procession start and end?
steps: It started at Karnak, Amun’s main temple.
It went to Luxor Temple, to the south.
Then the gods returned to Karnak.
blocks.a: From Karnak to Luxor Temple and back.

blocks.title: Who saw the god?
blocks.q: Ordinary people could not enter the sanctuary. How did they meet Amun at Opet?
steps: The statue traveled in its boat-shrine through the city.
The shrine was closed, but people saw the boat pass.
Crowds celebrated along the route and could ask the god questions.
blocks.a: They saw the god’s boat in the procession.

blocks.html: Thinking festivals took place only inside the temple. At Opet the god’s boat came out where crowds could see it. Quick check: a festival usually meant a procession.

The second great festival of Thebes took Amun across the river. Like The Opet Festival, it began at Karnak, but it led to the west bank, the side of the tombs and the memorial temples you met in Cult Temples and Memorial Temples.
In the Beautiful Festival of the Valley, Amun’s boat crossed the Nile to the temples of the west bank, and families visited the tombs of their dead and feasted there.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The Valley festival crossed from Karnak on the east bank to Deir el-Bahari and the memorial temples on the west bank.

items: The festival was held each year in the second month of Shemu, the harvest season, at the new moon.
Amun’s boat crossed the river and visited the memorial temples of the kings. In the 18th Dynasty its goal was Hatshepsut’s temple at Deir el-Bahari, in the bay of cliffs facing Karnak.
Families went to the tomb chapels of their relatives, with food, drink, music and flowers.
People spent the night at the tombs, sharing a meal with the dead.

blocks.html: Egyptians believed the dead lived on and still belonged to their families. When Amun visited the west bank, the living and the dead were brought together. A tomb was not a place to avoid but a house where the family could visit. Banquet scenes in Theban tombs, with guests, musicians and lotus flowers, recall these visits.
The festival is known from the Middle Kingdom, when Mentuhotep II built his temple at Deir el-Bahari, and it flourished in the New Kingdom.

head: Opet
Valley festival
blocks.cap: The two great festivals of Thebes.

blocks.title: Which festival?
blocks.q: A tomb painting shows a family feasting with musicians, and its text mentions Amun "when he crosses to the west". Which festival is likely?
steps: Amun crossing to the west bank fits the Valley festival.
A family feast at a tomb fits it too.
Opet stayed on the east bank.
blocks.a: The Beautiful Festival of the Valley.

blocks.title: Choosing a season
blocks.q: Opet fell in Akhet. When did the Valley festival fall?
steps: Egypt’s year had three seasons: Akhet (flood), Peret (growing), Shemu (harvest).
The Valley festival was in the second month of Shemu.
blocks.a: Shemu, the harvest season.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians avoided cemeteries. Families visited the tombs and shared meals with the dead, above all at this festival. Quick check: tomb chapels were built with open doors for visitors.

blocks.html: Egyptian beliefs about death grew from the ideas of order in Maat and Isfet and the story of Osiris in The Osiris Myth. Egyptians believed that death was not the end but a passage to a new life.
Egyptians believed death led to a new life, if the body was kept, the name remembered and offerings continued.

head: Need
Why
How it was met
rows: the parts of the person returned to it
a name spoken keeps its owner alive
names carved in the tomb, said by visitors
the dead still needed food and drink
family and priests brought them; texts and pictures made them last
blocks.cap: Three things the dead needed.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: rn, "name": the mouth (r) and the water ripple (n). A remembered name meant continued life.

blocks.html: The beliefs come from love of life, not fear of death. Egyptians pictured the next life as their own life made perfect: fields, family, feasts and the company of the gods. To reach it, the dead had to pass the judgment of Osiris, which looked at whether they had lived by maat. A person who passed was called mꜣꜥ-ḫrw, "true of voice", words written after the names of the dead.

The oldest religious texts, in the pyramids of the late Old Kingdom, describe the king’s afterlife: he rises to the sky, joins the sun god and becomes a star. In later periods more and more people hoped for the same blessed life. From the Middle Kingdom on, a justified dead person could be called "the Osiris N", joined with the god who had died and lived again. You will follow these texts in the unit on funerary texts.

blocks.title: Why carve a name?
blocks.q: Why might a tomb owner write his name dozens of times on the walls of his chapel?
steps: A name spoken kept its owner alive.
The more often it appears, the more likely it is to be read and remembered.
Visitors reading it aloud fed his memory, and so his life.
blocks.a: To keep his name, and himself, alive.

blocks.title: Reading a phrase
blocks.q: A stela reads, "the Osiris Senbi, true of voice". What two hopes does it express?
steps: "The Osiris" joins Senbi to the god who rose again.
"True of voice" says he passed the judgment.
Both are hopes for his new life.
blocks.a: Rebirth like Osiris, and a good verdict at the judgment.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians were obsessed with death. Their care for the dead came from love of life and the wish to go on living it. Quick check: look at what tombs show, which is mostly fields, food and family.

blocks.html: To live after death, as Beliefs About the Afterlife explained, a person needed body, name and offerings. Egyptians also believed that a person was made of several parts, each with its own role after death.

The ka was the life force, born with a person, which received the offerings; the ba could move about and was shown as a bird with a human head; the akh was the transfigured, effective spirit of the blessed dead. The name and the shadow were parts of the person too.

head: Part
Written with
Role
rows: life force; received offerings; could live in a statue
moved between tomb and world; shown in art as a human-headed bird
the blessed spirit, living among the gods and stars
kept the person alive while it was spoken
a dark copy that went with the person
blocks.cap: Parts of a person. Gods and kings could have many kas and bas.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The words for ka, ba and akh. The sign for ba is a stork, not the human-headed bird that art uses for it.

blocks.html: These parts let Egyptians say several things at once about the dead. The ka, born with each person (the god Khnum was said to shape it with the body), needed food, so offerings were made "for the ka of" the owner, and a ka statue gave it a home. The ba needed freedom, so it could fly out of the tomb by day and return to the body at night. The akh was what the dead became when everything went right: effective and shining, among the gods.

blocks.title: Which part eats?
blocks.q: An offering table is inscribed "for the ka of Hetepi". Why the ka?
steps: The ka was the life force that received offerings.
The food and drink nourished it.
So offerings were dedicated to the ka.
blocks.a: The ka received the offerings.

blocks.title: Sign or picture?
blocks.q: In a Book of the Dead papyrus, a bird with a human head flies down a tomb shaft. In the text below, the word for it is written with a stork. Is that a contradiction?
steps: The picture shows the ba as art pictured it.
The text writes the word bꜣ with the stork sign G29, which has the sound bꜣ.
The sign gives the sound; the picture gives the idea.
blocks.a: No: the stork spells the word; the human-headed bird shows the ba.

blocks.html: Equating the ba with the "soul" of later religions. Egyptian ideas divide a person differently, into several parts with different roles; one-word equivalents hide those differences. Quick check: say which part is meant and what it does.

blocks.html: The new life of Beliefs About the Afterlife was not automatic. The dead had to pass a judgment that looked at whether they had lived by maat. The best-known version is in spell 125 of the Book of the Dead. Of all the parts of a person, it is the heart that is tested.
The heart was weighed against the feather of Maat before Osiris. The dead declared that they had not done a list of wrongs; a monster, Ammit, waited for those who failed.

items: The dead person enters the Hall of the Two Truths.

Before 42 judges, he or she declares innocence of 42 wrongs: "I have not stolen", "I have not killed", "I have not told lies", and so on. Scholars call this the declaration of innocence, or "negative confession".
Anubis places the heart on one pan of a scale and the feather of Maat on the other.
Thoth, the scribe of the gods, writes down the result.
Ammit, "the Devourer", with a crocodile’s head, a lion’s front and a hippopotamus’s back, waits to eat a heart that fails.
If the scale balances, Horus leads the justified person to Osiris on his throne.

blocks.html: For Egyptians the heart was the seat of thought, memory and character, so it held a record of a whole life. A heart free of wrongdoing would weigh the same as truth itself. Spell 30B, often carved on the heart scarab placed on the mummy, asks the heart not to speak against its owner at the weighing.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: jb, "heart", and mꜣꜥt, "Maat": the two things on the scale.

blocks.title: Which way should the scale tip?
blocks.q: A painting shows the scale perfectly level. Did the dead person pass?
steps: The heart is weighed against the feather of Maat.
Passing means the two balance.
A level scale is balance.
blocks.a: Yes: balance means the heart was true.

blocks.title: Who does what?
blocks.q: Name the gods at the scale and their jobs.
steps: Anubis, the jackal-headed god, works the scale.
Thoth, the ibis-headed scribe, records the verdict.
Osiris, on his throne, receives the justified dead.
blocks.a: Anubis weighs, Thoth records, Osiris rules.

blocks.html: Thinking the heart had to be heavy, or light. It had to balance the feather: free of wrongdoing. Quick check: the image is a balance, so the goal is equal weight.

blocks.html: After the The Judgment of the Dead, where did the dead go? Egyptians pictured a realm called the Duat (dwꜣt), beyond the western horizon. The sun itself passed through it every night.
The Duat was the realm of the dead, through which the sun god sailed each night to be reborn at dawn.

items: At sunset the sun god entered the Duat in the west, often shown with a ram’s head, standing in his night boat.
He traveled through twelve regions, one for each hour of the night, with gates, guardians and crowds of the dead.
The serpent Apep (Apophis), enemy of order, tried to stop the boat; gods and spells overcame him.
In the deepest hour the sun united with Osiris, and both were renewed.
At dawn the sun was reborn in the east as Khepri, the scarab.

blocks.html: The idea joins two hopes. Every evening the sun seemed to die and every morning to be born again; Egyptians hoped the dead could share that cycle. Osiris gave the dead their new life; the sun gave light and movement. By meeting in the Duat, they made renewal complete. In another picture, the sky goddess Nut swallows the sun at evening and gives birth to it at dawn.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḫpr, "come into being": the scarab sign. As Khepri, the scarab was the newborn sun at dawn.

blocks.title: Counting the hours
blocks.q: The Duat was divided by the hours of the night. How many regions did the sun pass?
steps: The night had twelve hours.
One region per hour.
So twelve regions.

blocks.title: From night to day
blocks.q: In what forms did the sun god appear at evening, at midnight and at dawn on this journey?
steps: At evening he enters the Duat, often ram-headed, in his night boat.
At midnight he unites with Osiris.
At dawn he is reborn as Khepri.
blocks.a: Ram-headed at night, joined with Osiris at midnight, Khepri at dawn.

blocks.html: Picturing the Duat as an underground hell. It was a realm of passage and renewal, as well as danger; the blessed dead hoped to travel through it with the sun. Quick check: the journey ends in rebirth at dawn.
What did the justified dead hope for after the The Judgment of the Dead? One answer was the Field of Reeds (sḫt-jꜣrw), a perfect Egypt in the afterlife.
The blessed dead hoped to live in the Field of Reeds, a perfect Egypt where crops grew tall; shabti figures would do their work for them.

The vignette of Book of the Dead spell 110 is a map of the Field: canals and islands, the owner plowing, sowing and reaping, and boats on the water. The crops are huge, and there is plenty for all. It is the Nile valley, made perfect and lasting.

Egyptians knew one good life: farming by the river. So they pictured the best afterlife the same way. But a perfect Egypt still needed work, and in Egypt the state could call people to do labor on canals and fields. The dead might be called too. The answer was the shabti: a small figure, often mummy-shaped, holding hoes, that would answer for its owner.

items: Many shabtis carry spell 6 of the Book of the Dead: if the owner is called to work, the shabti says "Here I am!" and goes instead.
A later form of the name, ushabti, was understood as "answerer".
Some later burials had 365 workers, one for every day of the year, plus overseers to manage them.
They were made of wood, stone, and above all faience, a glazed material often blue or green.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: tꜣ, "land, earth": the flat land with grains of sand. The Field of Reeds was land like Egypt’s, only better.

blocks.title: A worker for each day
blocks.q: Why might a burial contain 365 shabtis?
steps: Each shabti could answer one call to work.
There are 365 days in the Egyptian year.
One worker per day covers the whole year.
blocks.a: One for each day of the year.

blocks.title: Reading a figure
blocks.q: A small blue faience figure is shaped like a mummy, holds two hoes and is inscribed with spell 6. What is it?
steps: Mummy shape and farm tools suggest work in the afterlife.
Spell 6 is the shabti spell.
So it is a shabti.
blocks.a: A shabti.

blocks.html: Thinking shabtis were toys or portraits. They were helpers meant to answer when the dead were called to work. Quick check: look for spell 6 and the farm tools.

sources.name: Book of the Dead, spells 6 and 110

blocks.html: The ka needed food and drink forever. Families and priests provided them at the tomb, at a special place: the false door.
Families and priests brought food and drink to a tomb’s false door and said the offering formula, so the dead would be fed. The false door was the meeting place of the living and the dead.

In an Old Kingdom mastaba chapel, the false door is a carved stone doorway that does not open. It shows the owner’s name and titles, often a picture of the owner seated at a table of bread, and the offering formula. Egyptians believed the dead could pass through it to receive what the living brought. An offering table stood in front of it.

The tomb had two parts with two purposes. The burial chamber, deep under the ground and sealed, protected the body. The chapel above stayed open, so the living could visit. The false door joined the two worlds: the dead came out, the living came in, and they met at the door. Words mattered as much as food: the offering formula, said aloud, was believed to provide what it named, even when no bread was there.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḥtp-dj-nsw, "an offering that the king gives", the start of the offering formula.

blocks.html: The formula asks for an "invocation offering", prt-ḫrw ("going forth of the voice"), of bread and beer, cattle and fowl, alabaster and linen, and "every good and pure thing" for the ka of the owner. Many tombs add an "appeal to the living", asking passers-by to say the formula. Wealthy families also paid ka-servants, priests given land or income, to keep the offerings going.

blocks.title: Feeding with words
blocks.q: A traveler passes an old tomb and reads its offering formula aloud. Why did the tomb owner want this?
steps: The spoken formula was believed to provide the offerings it named.
It cost the traveler nothing but breath.
So the dead were fed even without bread.
blocks.a: Saying the formula fed the dead.

blocks.title: Finding the door
blocks.q: In a mastaba chapel, which wall would you look at to find where the offerings were left?
steps: Look for the carved doorway that does not open.
It bears the owner’s name and the offering formula.
An offering table stands in front of it.
blocks.a: The false door.

blocks.html: Thinking the false door was a fake. It was the meeting place between the living and the dead. Quick check: look for the offering table in front of it.

blocks.html: In Beliefs About the Afterlife you saw that the dead needed a body to live on. Mummification was the careful work of keeping that body whole. This unit describes it plainly and calmly, as Egyptians saw it: an act of care for someone they loved.

Egyptians preserved the body so the ka and ba had a home to return to. Dry desert graves had first shown them that bodies could last. Full mummification was costly, and many people had simpler burials.

The parts of a person you met in The Ka, the Ba and the Akh were tied to the body. The ba flew out by day and came back to it at night; the ka lived in it and in the tomb statue. If the body was lost, these parts would lose their anchor. Preserving the body, and giving it a face and a name, protected the whole person.

In the Predynastic Period, people were buried in shallow pits in the desert sand. The hot, dry sand dried the bodies quickly, and some survive today, like the man from Gebelein in the British Museum, more than five thousand years old. Egyptians who saw such remains could see that a body could last. Later, when bodies were placed in coffins and tombs away from the sand, they no longer dried by themselves, and people developed ways to preserve them on purpose. By the 4th Dynasty, embalmers were already removing and storing internal organs: the oldest known stored organs belonged to Queen Hetepheres I, the mother of Khufu.

Full mummification took weeks of skilled work and costly materials. The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BC, describes three grades of treatment at different prices. Kings, officials and their families had the best; many ordinary people had simpler preparation, or were buried in the sand as their ancestors had been. Animals were mummified too, as pets and as offerings to gods.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: The name of Anubis, jnpw, god of embalming: j, n, p and w, with the jackal as determinative.

blocks.title: Why the desert mattered
blocks.q: Why did the earliest Egyptian bodies survive without any embalming?
steps: They were buried in hot, dry sand.
The sand drew water from the body quickly.
Without water, the body did not decay.
blocks.a: The dry sand preserved them naturally.

blocks.title: Grades of care
blocks.q: A family could not afford the most expensive embalming. What were its choices?
steps: Herodotus says there were three grades of treatment, at different prices.
A family could choose a simpler, cheaper one.
Many people had simple burials, but still with care and grave goods.
blocks.a: A cheaper grade, or a simpler burial.

blocks.html: Thinking all Egyptians were mummified. Full mummification was costly; many people had simpler burials. Quick check: ask who could pay for weeks of skilled work.

blocks.html: Building on Why Mummify?, this lesson follows the work of the embalmers. It took place in a workshop near the cemetery, under the protection of Anubis, and was done with care and prayers.
Embalmers removed the internal organs, dried the body with natron salt for about forty days, then anointed it and wrapped it in linen with amulets. The whole process took about seventy days.

items: The body was washed.
The brain was removed and not kept; Egyptians did not think it important.
The internal organs (the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines) were removed through a cut in the side and preserved separately. The heart was usually left in place.
The body was covered with natron, a natural salt from places like the Wadi Natrun, for about forty days, until it was dry.
It was then cleaned, packed to keep its shape, and rubbed with oils and resins.
It was wrapped in many layers of linen, with amulets placed among them and prayers said at each stage.
The mummy was placed in its coffin, and a ceremony called the Opening of the Mouth restored its senses for the new life.

blocks.html: Each step served the belief. Drying stopped decay, because decay needs water. The heart stayed because Egyptians saw it as the seat of thought and memory, needed at the judgment; the brain did not seem to matter. Oils and resins made the body fragrant and protected it. Linen and amulets wrapped it in protection. Seventy days gave time for all of it and matched the period of mourning.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: jb, "heart", the organ left in the body: Egyptians saw it as the seat of thought.

blocks.title: Adding up the days
blocks.q: Drying in natron took about 40 days, and the anointing and wrapping about 30 more. About how long did it all take?
steps: Seventy days is the traditional span from death to burial.
blocks.a: About 70 days.

blocks.title: Which organ stayed?
blocks.q: Why did embalmers leave the heart in the body?
steps: The heart was the seat of thought and memory.
It would be weighed in the judgment.
So it had to stay with its owner.
blocks.a: It was needed for the judgment.

blocks.html: Thinking the brain was kept with care. Embalmers did not keep it; Egyptians saw the heart, which was usually left in place, as the seat of thought. Quick check: the organ kept in the body is the one weighed at the judgment.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Opening of the mouth ceremony" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: The embalmers preserved the organs as well as the body. Both were then placed in containers that protected them and gave them meaning.
The organs went into four canopic jars guarded by the Four Sons of Horus; the body lay in nested coffins, sometimes with a mask over the face.

head: Son of Horus
Head on the lid
Organ
blocks.cap: The Four Sons of Horus and the organs they guarded. Each was protected in turn by a goddess: Isis, Nephthys, Neith and Selket.

blocks.html: Each organ was part of the person and had to be kept for the new life, so each received a guardian. The four sons were also linked with the four directions, wrapping the person in protection on every side. In the Middle Kingdom and early New Kingdom, all four lids usually had human heads; the four different heads became the rule later in the New Kingdom.

items: Old and Middle Kingdom coffins were often rectangular boxes, with a pair of eyes painted on one side so the dead, lying on their side, could look out toward the east and the rising sun.
From the Middle Kingdom on, coffins shaped like a wrapped body, with an idealized face, became common. The coffin was a second, perfect body.
Coffins could be nested one inside another, and the whole set placed in a stone sarcophagus.
A mask over the mummy’s face gave it a lasting, divine face. Gold was used because it never tarnishes, like the flesh of the gods.

blocks.html: Tutankhamun’s burial shows the system at its richest: four gilded shrines, a stone sarcophagus, three nested coffins (the innermost of solid gold) and the famous gold mask inlaid with glass and stones.

blocks.name: eg-cartouche
blocks.cap: Tutankhamun’s birth name, twt-ꜥnḫ-jmn, "living image of Amun".

blocks.title: Matching a lid
blocks.q: A canopic jar has a lid shaped like a jackal’s head. What did it hold, and who guarded it?
steps: A jackal head is Duamutef.
Duamutef guarded the stomach.
blocks.a: The stomach, guarded by Duamutef.

blocks.title: Reading a coffin
blocks.q: A rectangular Middle Kingdom coffin has two eyes painted on one long side. Which way did the mummy face?
steps: The eyes were placed where the face was.
The body lay on its left side.
It faced the eyes, toward the east.
blocks.a: Toward the painted eyes, to the east.

blocks.html: Mixing up the canopic jars’ lids. The Four Sons of Horus have human (Imsety), baboon (Hapy), jackal (Duamutef) and falcon (Qebehsenuef) heads. Quick check: "Imsety is the only human."
