blocks.html: The beliefs about the Beliefs About the Afterlife are known best from texts written for the dead. The oldest are the Pyramid Texts. They appear in the late Old Kingdom, after the age of the great sun kings you met in The Sun Kings and the Pyramid Texts.
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest Egyptian religious texts: spells carved inside pyramids from Unas, at the end of the 5th Dynasty, onward, to help the king rise to the sky.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Old Kingdom: Djoser and Khufu built pyramids without texts; Unas was the first to carve them inside, and 6th Dynasty kings like Pepi II followed.

items: The spells were carved in columns of hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial chamber and the rooms and passages near it, often filled with blue or green paint.
Unas’s pyramid at Saqqara is the first. The kings of the 6th Dynasty, some of their queens, and a king of the 8th Dynasty followed.
They were not decoration for visitors: once the tomb was sealed, no living person was meant to read them.
Kurt Sethe published them in 1908–1922 and numbered them as "utterances"; scholars still use his numbers.

blocks.html: Why carve spells by the body? Words were believed to act. Carved in stone beside the king, the spells would go on working for him forever, even if no priest came. Many speak as if the rites are happening now: the king is purified, fed, raised up; he climbs to the sky, sails with Ra, joins the stars that never set, and is Osiris. Some spells are older than Unas and may have been spoken at royal funerals long before they were carved.

blocks.title: Dating the first texts
blocks.q: Khufu’s reign ended c. 2566 BC, and Unas began to reign c. 2375 BC. About how long after Khufu do the Pyramid Texts begin?
steps: 191 years is about two centuries.
blocks.a: About two centuries.

blocks.title: Where to look
blocks.q: A visitor enters the Great Pyramid of Khufu expecting to see the Pyramid Texts. What will she find?
steps: Khufu’s chambers have no religious texts.
The texts begin with Unas, at Saqqara.
She should visit Unas’s pyramid instead.
blocks.a: No texts; they start with Unas.

blocks.html: Thinking the Great Pyramid has texts inside. The Pyramid Texts start about two centuries later, with Unas. Quick check: Khufu is 4th Dynasty; Unas ends the 5th.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Pyramid of Unas" (current consensus and dates)
Ian Shaw, ed., The Oxford History of Ancient Egypt (2000): dates, as in Wikipedia’s "Egyptian chronology"

blocks.html: After the Old Kingdom, the hope of the The Pyramid Texts spread beyond the king. In the First Intermediate Period and the Middle Kingdom, officials and their families had afterlife spells painted inside their wooden coffins. Scholars call these the Coffin Texts.
In the Middle Kingdom, spells were painted inside the coffins of officials, so people who were not royal could use them too.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: Three great collections of spells, one after another: Pyramid Texts, Coffin Texts, Book of the Dead.

items: The spells were written in ink in columns, around the inside of the coffin, close to the body.
Many adapt Pyramid Texts spells for a non-royal owner; many are new.
Adriaan de Buck’s edition (1935–1961) numbers 1,185 spells.
Some coffins from Deir el-Bersha have the Book of Two Ways painted on the floor: a map of two routes through the afterlife.
The best-known coffins come from the cemeteries of provincial governors, at places like Deir el-Bersha, Beni Hasan and Asyut.

blocks.html: Why did the spells spread? After the Old Kingdom, power and wealth spread to the provinces, and local governors and officials built rich tombs of their own. They wanted the same protection the king had. A coffin was a good place for it: it was always close to the body, and painting was quicker and cheaper than carving a pyramid.

Older books call this change "the democratization of the afterlife". The phrase is now debated. The coffins belonged to the elite, not to everyone, and some scholars argue that well-off people already hoped for such an afterlife before the spells were written down for them.

blocks.title: Royal or not?
blocks.q: A painted wooden coffin of a Middle Kingdom official is covered inside with spells. What are they?
steps: Wooden coffin, painted inside, Middle Kingdom, non-royal owner.
That fits the Coffin Texts.
blocks.a: Coffin Texts.

blocks.title: Weighing a phrase
blocks.q: A textbook says the Coffin Texts "gave everyone the afterlife". How would you improve the sentence?
steps: The coffins belonged to officials and their families.
Ordinary farmers did not have them.
The term "democratization" is debated.
blocks.a: Say the spells reached the elite beyond the king.

blocks.html: Thinking only kings had afterlife texts in all periods. By the Middle Kingdom, officials did too. Quick check: look at the owner’s title on the coffin.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Book of Two Ways" (current consensus and dates)
Adriaan de Buck, The Egyptian Coffin Texts (7 vols., 1935–1961)

blocks.html: In the New Kingdom, the spells of the The Coffin Texts gave way to a new form: spells written on papyrus rolls placed in the tomb. We call them the Book of the Dead.

From the New Kingdom, spells for the journey through the afterlife were written on papyrus rolls placed in the tomb. Egyptians called them "spells for going forth by day", and each roll was a selection made for its owner.

The Egyptian title, rw nw prt m hrw, means "spells for going forth by day": the dead hoped to leave the tomb by day and move freely. The modern name comes from the German scholar Karl Richard Lepsius, who published a long papyrus in Turin in 1842 as the Todtenbuch, "Book of the Dead", and numbered its spells.

head: Spell
What it does
rows: tells a shabti to work for its owner
asks the heart not to speak against its owner (often on heart scarabs)
the Field of Reeds, with its map
the judgment and the declarations of innocence
blocks.cap: Some well-known spells, in Lepsius’s numbering.

blocks.html: Why papyrus? A roll could hold many spells and colored pictures (vignettes), was easier to make than painted coffins, and could be ordered to suit the buyer. Workshops made rolls in advance with blank spaces for the owner’s name; a buyer chose what he could afford. That is why no two rolls are the same: about two hundred spells are known, but each roll has a selection.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: hrw, "day", the last word of the title "spells for going forth by day". The sun is its determinative.

blocks.title: Filling in the name
blocks.q: A Book of the Dead roll has empty spaces where the owner’s name should be. What does that suggest?
steps: Workshops made rolls in advance.
The buyer’s name was to be added later.
Sometimes it never was.
blocks.a: It was made ready-made, for sale.

blocks.title: One book or many?
blocks.q: Two rolls from the same century have different spells in a different order. Is one of them a bad copy?
steps: Each roll was a selection, made for its owner.
There was no single fixed book.
Different selections are normal.
blocks.a: No: each roll was its own selection.

blocks.html: Thinking the Book of the Dead was one fixed book. Each roll was a selection of spells, made for its owner. Quick check: Egyptians said "spells", plural, not "the book".

Karl Richard Lepsius, Das Todtenbuch der Ägypter (1842)

blocks.html: Besides the spells of the The Book of the Dead, New Kingdom kings had their tombs painted with long illustrated guides to the night journey of the sun through the The Duat and the Sun's Night Journey. Scholars call them the books of the underworld.
New Kingdom royal tombs show the sun’s night journey hour by hour, in books like the Amduat, "What Is in the Underworld". They are not the Book of the Dead.

head: Book
Where it first appears
How it divides the night
rows: royal tombs of the early 18th Dynasty; complete in Thutmose III’s tomb
twelve hours, each ending at a gate
blocks.cap: Three books of the underworld.

blocks.html: The king hoped to share the sun’s cycle: to enter the Duat at evening, travel through its twelve hours, unite with Osiris in the deepest hour and rise at dawn. Painting the whole journey on his tomb walls gave him a map and made the journey happen for him, night after night. The Amduat names the gods, the dangers and the dead in each hour, so the one who knows it can pass.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḫpr, "come into being": in the twelfth hour of the Amduat the sun becomes Khepri, the scarab, and rises.

blocks.html: In the tomb of Thutmose III (KV34), the Amduat runs around the oval burial chamber in simple line drawings, as if a giant papyrus had been unrolled on the walls. After the New Kingdom, private people could own copies on papyrus too.

blocks.title: Telling them apart
blocks.q: A tomb wall in the Valley of the Kings shows the sun’s boat moving through twelve sections of the night. Is it the Book of the Dead?
steps: A journey of the sun through twelve hours describes the Amduat (or the Book of Gates).
It is on a royal tomb wall.
The Book of the Dead is spells on papyrus for many people.
blocks.a: No: it is an underworld book such as the Amduat.

blocks.title: Reading the name
blocks.q: What does "Amduat" tell you about the book?
steps: Amduat comes from jmj-dwꜣt, "what is in the Duat".
It describes the underworld and its beings.
So it is a guide to the Duat.
blocks.a: It is a guide to what is in the underworld.

blocks.html: Confusing the Amduat (royal tombs, the sun’s journey) with the Book of the Dead (papyri for many people, spells for the dead person’s own needs). Quick check: ask whose journey it describes, the sun’s or the owner’s.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Book of Gates" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: A tomb had two jobs, as you saw in Beliefs About the Afterlife: protect the body and let the living bring offerings. The earliest great tombs did both in a simple shape, the mastaba.
Early elite tombs were mastabas: low, flat-topped buildings over a burial shaft, with a chapel for offerings. Mastabas came first; the first pyramid began as one.

head: Part
What it was for
rows: the flat-topped building above ground, of mud brick or stone
deep below, holding the body; filled in after the burial
a room open to visitors, with the false door and the offering table
a closed room for the statue of the dead, with a slit to "see" the offerings
blocks.cap: The parts of an Old Kingdom mastaba.

blocks.html: The shape follows the two jobs. The body needed safety, so it went deep underground and the shaft was blocked. The ka needed food, so the chapel stayed open above. The word mastaba is Arabic for "bench": the low tombs with sloping sides look like the mud-brick benches outside village houses.

Kings and nobles of the Early Dynastic Period had tombs of this kind at Abydos and Saqqara. In the 3rd Dynasty, Djoser’s architect Imhotep built a square stone mastaba at Saqqara and then enlarged it in stages, stacking smaller layers on top, until it became the Step Pyramid of six steps. Officials went on building mastabas around the royal pyramids; the decorated chapels of Ti and Mereruka at Saqqara are among the finest.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: Djoser’s Step Pyramid at Saqqara: six stone steps, grown from a mastaba.

blocks.title: Where is the body?
blocks.q: Visitors walked into a mastaba’s chapel. Did they see the coffin?
steps: The coffin lay in a burial chamber at the bottom of a shaft.
The shaft was filled in after the burial.
The chapel above was for offerings, not for the body.
blocks.a: No: the body was far below, sealed away.

blocks.title: Which came first?
blocks.q: A friend says the Egyptians built pyramids first and mastabas later, as a cheaper copy. How do you answer?
steps: Early Dynastic tombs were mastaba-like.
The first pyramid, Djoser’s, began as a mastaba in the 3rd Dynasty.
Officials kept building mastabas alongside the pyramids.
blocks.a: Mastabas came first.

blocks.html: Thinking pyramids came first. Mastabas came first, and the first pyramid began as a mastaba. Quick check: the Step Pyramid is a stack of mastaba-like layers.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Pyramid of Djoser" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: The Sneferu, Khufu and the True Pyramid produced Egypt’s most famous buildings. A pyramid, though, was never meant to stand alone. Growing from the Mastaba Tombs, it became the center of a whole complex of temples.
A pyramid stood in a complex: a valley temple by the river, a covered causeway, and a mortuary temple against the pyramid, with smaller pyramids and boat pits around it.

items: Valley temple: at the edge of the flood plain, reached by boat along a canal. The body may have been received here.
Causeway: a covered, often decorated corridor climbing to the desert plateau.
Mortuary temple: against the east side of the pyramid, where daily offerings for the king were made.
Pyramid: the tomb, with its entrance usually on the north side.
Around it: queens’ pyramids, a small satellite pyramid, boat pits and an enclosure wall, with officials’ mastabas nearby.

blocks.name: eg-pyramid
blocks.cap: The great pyramids side by side, to scale: Djoser’s Step Pyramid, Sneferu’s Bent and Red Pyramids, and the three at Giza.

blocks.html: The complex followed the path of the king’s cult. Boats brought people and goods from the river to the valley temple; the causeway led up to the mortuary temple, where priests served the king’s ka forever; the pyramid held his body and joined him to the sky and the sun. The pyramid’s shape may recall the benben and the sun’s rays, as you saw in The First Mound, though Egyptians did not write down one explanation.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: The pyramid fields near Memphis: Giza, Abusir, Saqqara and Dahshur.

blocks.title: Following the path
blocks.q: Put these in order from the river: mortuary temple, causeway, pyramid, valley temple.
steps: Start at the river: the valley temple.
Climb the causeway.
Reach the mortuary temple, then the pyramid.
blocks.a: Valley temple, causeway, mortuary temple, pyramid.

blocks.title: Which is taller?
blocks.q: From the ground, Khafre’s pyramid looks taller than Khufu’s. Is it?
steps: Khufu’s was about 146.6 m tall when built; Khafre’s about 143.5 m.
Khafre’s stands on higher ground and keeps some casing near the top.
So it only looks taller.
blocks.a: No: Khufu’s was taller.

blocks.html: Picturing pyramids standing alone in the sand. Each was the center of temples, a causeway and smaller pyramids. Quick check: look for the causeway running down toward the valley.

blocks.html: After the pyramid age, tombs took a new form. From the Middle Kingdom on, many were cut into cliffs, and New Kingdom kings were buried in hidden rock-cut tombs.
Rock-cut tombs were carved into cliffs: Middle Kingdom governors at Beni Hasan, New Kingdom kings in the Valley of the Kings at Thebes. Why kings gave up pyramids is debated.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Western Thebes: the Valley of the Kings, the Valley of the Queens, the workmen’s village of Deir el-Medina and the memorial temples along the edge of the fields.

items: Beni Hasan, in Middle Egypt: tombs of 11th and 12th Dynasty governors, cut high in the cliffs and painted with farming, crafts, wrestling and hunting.

The Valley of the Kings: from early in the 18th Dynasty (probably Thutmose I) to the end of the 20th, kings cut long corridors and chambers into the valley’s rock. Tutankhamun’s tomb, KV62, was found nearly intact by Howard Carter in 1922.

blocks.html: The cliffs offered solid rock that could be carved deep and decorated inside, and in the Valley of the Kings the tomb entrances could be hidden. In the New Kingdom, the king’s tomb and his memorial temple were split: the tomb in the valley, the temple on the plain, where priests could reach it every day. Skilled crews from the village of Deir el-Medina cut and painted the royal tombs.

Ahmose I, the first king of the New Kingdom, built the last royal pyramid in Egypt, at Abydos. Scholars weigh several reasons for the change: pyramids had been robbed, so a hidden tomb might be safer; pyramids were very costly; and beliefs about the afterlife had changed. The pyramid-shaped peak above the Valley of the Kings may also have made the place fitting. None of these is certain on its own.

blocks.title: Which site?
blocks.q: A tomb of a 12th Dynasty governor, cut into a cliff and painted with wrestlers and craftsmen, is most likely at:
steps: 12th Dynasty: Middle Kingdom.
Governors’ rock-cut tombs with daily life scenes: Beni Hasan.
blocks.a: Beni Hasan.

blocks.title: Weighing reasons
blocks.q: A guide says, "Kings stopped building pyramids because they were too hard." Is that the whole story?
steps: Egyptians had built pyramids for a thousand years, so skill was not the problem.
Theft, cost and changing beliefs are all argued.
The reasons are debated.
blocks.a: No: several reasons are debated.

blocks.html: Thinking pyramids were given up only because they were too hard to build. Theft and changing beliefs both played a part, and the reasons are debated. Quick check: give at least two reasons and say they are debated.

blocks.html: The walls of the rock-cut tombs and mastaba chapels are covered with scenes: plowing, harvest, fishing, cattle, crafts, banquets and long tables of offerings. These pictures had a job to do.
Tomb scenes of farming, feasting and offering were meant to provide for the dead forever, not only to record their lives. They show an ideal life for eternity.

Egyptians believed that images and words could act. A picture of bread on an offering table could feed the ka; a picture of servants harvesting grain could keep the harvest coming. Carved or painted in the tomb, these images would go on working after the family stopped visiting. That is why the same themes repeat in tomb after tomb: they are the things a person needs, not a diary of one life.

blocks.text: Signs that images were believed to act

items: The owner is shown again and again seated before a table piled with food, often with a long list of offerings.
In some burial chambers, signs of dangerous animals like snakes and scorpions are drawn cut in two, so they could not harm the dead.
Enemies sometimes hacked out the faces or names of figures, to stop the images from working for their owners.
Scenes show everything in its best state: full granaries, fat cattle, a young and healthy owner.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḥtp, "offering": the sign is a loaf of bread on a reed mat, the picture of an offering table.

blocks.html: The scenes still tell us much about daily life, because artists drew real tools, crops and crafts. But read them as an ideal, not a snapshot: a scene of a harvest does not prove that this harvest happened on a given day.

blocks.title: Snapshot or ideal?
blocks.q: A tomb shows its owner, young and slim, watching a perfect harvest, though his mummy shows he died old. What does that mean?
steps: The scene shows the life he wished to have forever.
It is an ideal, not a portrait of a day.
Age and illness are left out on purpose.
blocks.a: It is an ideal image for eternity.

blocks.title: Why cut the snake?
blocks.q: In a burial chamber, a hieroglyph of a snake is drawn in two pieces. Why?
steps: Egyptians believed images could come to life.
A whole snake next to the body might harm it.
Cutting it made it harmless.
blocks.a: To keep the image from harming the dead.

blocks.html: Reading tomb scenes as snapshots of real events. They show an ideal life for eternity. Quick check: ask what the scene provides for the dead.

blocks.html: The Why Tombs Were Decorated were meant to work forever. To do that, every figure had to be complete and clear. Egyptian artists followed rules that made this possible, and the first rule is about how a body is shown.
Artists drew each part of a figure from its most typical view: the face in profile, the eye from the front, the shoulders from the front, the legs and feet in profile.

head: Part
Shown
blocks.cap: How a standing figure is put together.

blocks.html: Why combine views? The profile shows the shape of the nose, lips and chin best; an eye seen from the side is a sliver, so the eye is drawn whole, from the front. Shoulders seen from the front show both arms clearly. Legs in profile show the stride. The aim was not to copy what one viewer sees from one spot, but to show each part as it is known to be, complete. Scholars call this "aspective" (or composite) representation, as opposed to perspective.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: rmṯ, "people": the seated man and woman at the end are drawn by the same rules as large figures, with heads in profile.

blocks.html: The same rule applies to things. In a garden scene from the tomb chapel of Nebamun, the pool is drawn from above, as a rectangle full of fish and ducks, while the trees around it are drawn from the side. On an offering table, the loaves and jars are stacked above the tabletop so that none hides another.

blocks.title: Reading a pool
blocks.q: A painting shows a rectangular pool seen from above, with trees lying flat around its edges. Is the painter confused?
steps: A pool is clearest from above, as its shape.
A tree is clearest from the side.
Each thing is drawn in its most typical view.
blocks.a: No: each thing is shown in its clearest view.

blocks.title: Checking a figure
blocks.q: A drawing shows a man’s face in profile with the eye in profile too. Is that the classic convention?
steps: In the convention, the face is in profile.
But the eye is drawn from the front.
So this drawing breaks the rule.
blocks.a: No: the classic eye is frontal.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptians could not draw perspective. They chose to show each part clearly, as they knew it to be; sketches on flakes of stone (ostraca) show they could draw freely. Quick check: ask what the rule makes clearer.

blocks.html: Besides the composite view, Egyptian artists kept figures in fixed proportions. To do so they drew on a grid of squares.
Artists drew figures on a grid: a standing figure was 18 squares from the soles to the hairline. A later grid, from the 25th and 26th Dynasties, used 21 squares from the soles to the upper eyelid.

A grid keeps proportions the same at any size. If a figure is 18 squares tall, it has the same shape whether each square is 1 cm or 10 cm. An artist could draw a small sketch on a grid and copy it square by square onto a large grid on a wall. Many hands could work on one tomb, and the figures would still match. In the Old Kingdom artists used a few guide lines at set heights; full square grids appear in the Middle Kingdom.

head: Classic grid
Later grid
blocks.cap: Two grids (after Gay Robins’s studies of proportion).

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: z, "man": the seated man is a determinative. Large figures followed grid proportions; small signs followed the same models.

blocks.html: Unfinished tombs and drawing boards still show the red grid lines under the figures, sometimes with the artist’s first sketch and the corrections in black.

blocks.title: Height on the wall
blocks.q: A standing figure is drawn on the classic grid with squares 4 cm wide. How tall is it from the soles to the hairline?
steps: The figure is 18 squares tall.
blocks.a: 72 cm.

blocks.title: Finding the square
blocks.q: A standing figure measures 90 cm from the soles to the hairline on the classic grid. How wide is each square?
steps: The figure spans 18 squares.
blocks.a: 5 cm.

blocks.title: Scaling up
blocks.q: A sketch on 2 cm squares is copied onto a wall grid of 8 cm squares. How many times bigger is the copy?
steps: The copy keeps the same number of squares.
Each square is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 times wider.
So the copy is 4 times as tall.
blocks.a: 4 times.

blocks.html: Thinking the grid was invented by modern scholars. Grid lines survive on unfinished ancient walls. Quick check: look for the red lines in photos of unfinished tombs.

blocks.html: With the composite view, artists made each figure clear. With size, they made each figure’s importance clear.
The most important figure is the largest: the king larger than his enemies, a tomb owner larger than his servants. In Egyptian art, size shows rank, not height or distance.

Egyptian art did not try to show a scene as one person would see it from one spot, so it did not need distant figures to look small. Size was free to carry another meaning: importance. A king smiting his enemies towers over them because he is the king. Scholars call this hierarchic scale.

head: Scene
Largest
Smaller
rows: often the husband, the tomb owner
wife and children, though wives can be shown as large
blocks.cap: Hierarchic scale in common scenes.

blocks.html: The rule is very old. On the Narmer Palette, one of the first royal monuments, King Narmer strides across the scene and strikes a kneeling enemy who is much smaller; the sandal-bearer behind him and the fallen enemies below are smaller too. Three thousand years later, temple pylons of the Ptolemies show the same picture.

blocks.name: eg-map
blocks.cap: Hierakonpolis, where the Narmer Palette was found. On it, King Narmer is the largest figure, striking an enemy.

blocks.title: Who matters most?
blocks.q: A tomb wall shows one man three times taller than the farmers plowing beside him. Who is he?
steps: Size shows rank.
In a tomb, the largest figure is usually the owner.
The farmers are his workers.
blocks.a: The tomb owner.

blocks.title: Not distance
blocks.q: In a scene, a small figure stands next to a large one on the same ground line. Is the small one farther away?
steps: Both stand on the same ground line.
Egyptian art used size for rank.
So the small figure is less important, not farther away.
blocks.a: No: it is of lower rank.

blocks.html: Reading size as height or distance. In Egyptian art, size shows rank. Quick check: find the largest figure and ask who that person is.
Wives are sometimes shown as large as their husbands, especially in pair statues. When a wife is smaller, it usually marks whose tomb or monument it is.

blocks.html: Most Egyptian art was painted, as you will see in Painting and Pigments. Its colors followed rules too, building on the conventions of drawing, and each color could carry meaning.
Colors carried meaning: black for fertile soil and rebirth, green for growth and new life, red for energy or danger, gold for the flesh of the gods.

head: Color
Linked with
rows: the dark Nile mud, fertility and rebirth; Egypt was kmt, the Black Land
the desert (dšrt, the Red Land), energy, fire and danger; also Seth
the sun and the flesh of the gods, which never decays
the sky and the water; the gods’ hair was said to be of lapis lazuli
blocks.cap: Colors and what they could mean. Meaning depended on context.

blocks.html: The meanings came from Egypt’s land. The flood left black mud in which crops grew green; the desert beyond was red and dangerous. So black and green stood for life and rebirth, red for both power and threat. Gold does not tarnish, so it suited the gods’ eternal bodies. Osiris, the god who rose again, is often painted with black or green skin for this reason.

Some colors were conventions of figure drawing. Men were usually painted with reddish-brown skin and women with lighter, yellowish skin. This was a rule of the art, not a portrait of anyone’s real skin. Scribes wrote headings in red ink and the rest in black.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nbw, "gold": a collar of beads. Gold was the flesh of the gods.

blocks.title: Reading Osiris
blocks.q: Why is Osiris often green?
steps: Green is the color of growing plants.
Osiris died and came back to life.
His color shows rebirth.
blocks.a: Green stands for new life.

blocks.title: Red and danger
blocks.q: In some papyri, the name of the serpent Apep is written in red. Why?
steps: Red could mark danger.
Apep was the enemy of the sun.
Red sets the hostile name apart.
blocks.a: Red marks a dangerous being.

blocks.html: Thinking black skin on Osiris shows his origin. Black and green showed rebirth and the fertile soil. Quick check: ask what the color meant in Egypt, not what it means today.

sources.name: Wikipedia, "Art of ancient Egypt" (current consensus and dates)

blocks.html: The Composite Views governs one figure. Registers govern a whole wall.
Scenes run in horizontal bands called registers, each with its own ground line. Read them band by band, like lines of text. Figures, like hieroglyphs, face the way the text begins.

Because Egyptian art did not use one-point perspective, it needed another way to show many activities at once. Registers solved it: each band is a strip of the world, with its own ground. A harvest wall can show plowing in one band, reaping in the next and storing grain in the next, in order. The top band is not farther away; it is the next row.

items: Each register stands on its own ground line.
Read the bands one after another, usually from top to bottom.
A large figure of the tomb owner often stands at the side, spanning several bands, watching over all of them.
Figures and hieroglyphs face toward the start of the text. If they face right, read from right to left.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḥqꜣ, "ruler", written right to left: the seated man faces right, toward the start of the line, and the arrow shows the reading direction.

blocks.html: The same rule of direction joins the pictures and the writing. In a scene, the captions and the figures they describe face the same way, so a reader can tell which words belong to whom.

blocks.title: Which way to read?
blocks.q: In a line of hieroglyphs, the owl and the seated man face left. Where does the line start?
steps: Signs face the start of the line.
They face left.
So the line starts at the left.
blocks.a: At the left; read left to right.

blocks.title: Rows or depth?
blocks.q: A wall has three bands: plowing at the top, reaping in the middle, threshing at the bottom. Is the plowing farther away?
steps: Each band has its own ground line.
Bands are rows, read like lines of text.
They show steps of the work in order.
blocks.a: No: each band is its own row.

blocks.html: Reading registers as a single scene in depth. Each band is its own row, read like lines of text. Quick check: find the ground line under each band.

blocks.html: Statues followed the same ideals as drawings, and the grid of proportions was used for them too: sculptors drew the figure on the faces of the stone block before cutting. A small set of poses covers most Egyptian statues.
Common types are the seated statue, the standing striding statue (left foot forward), the scribe statue, the block statue and the pair statue.

head: Type
Pose
Example
rows: on a block seat, hands on the knees, looking ahead
Khafre, with the falcon Horus behind his head
left foot forward, arms at the sides, a back pillar
cross-legged, a papyrus roll open on the lap
the Seated Scribe in the Louvre
squatting, knees up, wrapped in a cloak: a cube with a head
common from the Middle Kingdom on
husband and wife side by side, often an arm around the other
Menkaure and his queen, from Giza
blocks.cap: Five common kinds of statue.

blocks.html: Statues were not mainly portraits for people to admire. A statue in the serdab of a mastaba gave the ka a body to dwell in and receive offerings. A statue set up in a temple let its owner share in the god’s offerings and stay near the god forever. So the poses were the ones that suited those roles: calm, upright, ready to receive, and solid enough to last. The block statue, almost a cube, was ideal for a temple court and for carrying long inscriptions on its flat sides.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: mn, "remain, endure": what statues were for. The game board writes mn; the ripple of water repeats n.

blocks.title: Naming the pose
blocks.q: A limestone figure sits cross-legged with a papyrus roll on his lap. Which kind of statue is it?
steps: Cross-legged, with papyrus: the pose of a scribe at work.
It shows the owner as a man of learning.
blocks.a: A scribe statue.

blocks.title: Reading the stride
blocks.q: A standing statue of an official has his left foot forward. Is he walking?
steps: Standing statues of men are made with the left foot forward.
The weight is still balanced on both feet.
It is a convention, not a moment of walking.
blocks.a: No: it is the standard pose.

blocks.html: Thinking the forward left foot shows walking. It is a convention of standing statues of men; women are usually shown with their feet closer together. Quick check: the figure stands still against its back pillar.

blocks.html: Most temple and tomb walls were decorated in relief: carved, then painted. Relief carving builds on the same rules as statues and drawings, but there are two ways to carve it.
Raised relief cuts away the background so the figure stands out; sunk relief cuts the figure into the wall and suits bright sun outdoors.

head: Raised relief
Sunk relief
rows: the figure itself, below the flat wall
the figure stands above the surface
the edges of the figure go into the stone
strong sun outdoors, which casts sharp shadows
quicker; harder to erase or recarve
blocks.cap: Raised and sunk relief compared.

blocks.html: The choice followed the light. In a dim room, a raised figure shows its gentle modeling. Outside in the hard Egyptian sun, a raised figure can look flat, but the deep cut edges of sunk relief throw strong shadows and make it readable from far away. Ramesses II had many reliefs cut in deep sunk relief, even indoors; it was faster, and deep cuts are hard for a later king to recarve with his own name.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nfr, "good, beautiful": a word often carved in both kinds of relief, in titles and names.

blocks.html: Both kinds were painted. The bare stone we see in most temples today has lost its paint to sun, rain, floods and time; in protected places, like some tombs and the inner rooms of temples, bright colors survive.

blocks.title: Indoors or out?
blocks.q: A battle scene covers the outside face of a temple pylon, in full sun. Which kind of relief would you expect?
steps: Outdoor wall in strong sun.
Sunk relief casts sharp shadows there.
blocks.a: Sunk relief.

blocks.title: Feeling the edges
blocks.q: You run your finger along a carved figure: the figure is lower than the wall around it. Which kind is it?
steps: The figure is below the surface.
That is sunk relief.
blocks.a: Sunk relief.

blocks.html: Confusing the two. In sunk relief, the edges of the figure go into the stone; in raised relief, the background is lowered. Quick check: is the flat original surface around the figure (sunk) or on the figure (raised)?

blocks.html: The meanings of color needed paints to carry them. Egyptian painters made their colors mostly from minerals and worked on plaster or smoothed stone.
Painters used mineral colors, including the first known synthetic pigment, Egyptian blue, on plaster or stone. Most Egyptian art was painted in bright colors.

head: Color
Made from
rows: malachite, a copper mineral, or ground green frit
Egyptian blue, made by heating sand, lime, copper and a flux
blocks.cap: The painter’s palette.

blocks.html: Mineral colors last. They do not fade in sunlight the way many plant dyes do, which suited art made for eternity. Blue minerals like lapis lazuli were rare and costly, so Egyptians invented a way to make blue: heating sand, lime and copper with a little natron in a furnace, then grinding the blue glassy result. Egyptian blue is the first known synthetic pigment, and it was used for thousands of years.

items: The wall was smoothed. Poor stone or mud brick was coated with mud plaster and a thin white layer.
A grid and a sketch in red were drawn, then corrected in black.
Colors were mixed with a binder, such as plant gum, and laid on the dry plaster in flat areas. This is not fresco, which paints into wet plaster.
Brushes were made from reeds and palm fibers; fine outlines were added last.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: nbw, "gold", a collar of beads. Painters used yellow for gold, the color of the gods’ flesh.

blocks.title: Why make blue?
blocks.q: Why did Egyptians manufacture blue instead of grinding a blue stone?
steps: Blue stones like lapis lazuli were rare and imported.
Sand, lime and copper were easy to find.
Heating them made a lasting blue in quantity.
blocks.a: Egyptian blue was cheaper and plentiful.

blocks.title: Fresco or not?
blocks.q: A painting’s colors sit on top of a dry white layer, held by gum. Is it a fresco?
steps: A fresco is painted into wet plaster.
Here the plaster was dry and the color was held by a binder.
blocks.a: No: it was painted on dry plaster.

blocks.html: Thinking Egyptian art was the plain stone color we see today. Most was painted in bright colors; the paint has worn away. Quick check: look for traces of color in protected corners.
Some of the finest New Kingdom paintings come from the tomb chapel of Nebamun at Thebes, now in the British Museum: a garden pool, a banquet and a hunt in the marshes.

blocks.html: The rules you have learned held for three thousand years, with one striking break. Under Akhenaten, whose religious changes you met in Akhenaten and Amarna, art changed too. It built on the kinds of statues but gave them a new look.
Under Akhenaten, art changed: long faces, rounded bodies, family scenes, and the Aten’s rays ending in hands. What the style meant is debated.

items: Faces are long, with a long chin, narrow eyes and full lips.
Bodies have narrow shoulders, a rounded belly, wide hips and thin limbs.
The royal family is shown kissing, holding and playing with their daughters.
The Aten, the sun disk, sends down rays that end in hands, often holding the ankh to the noses of the king and queen.
Nature scenes on palace floors are lively and full of movement.

blocks.name: eg-timeline
blocks.cap: The Amarna age was short: Akhenaten’s reign (c. 1352–1336 BC), between Amenhotep III and Tutankhamun.

blocks.html: Why did art change? Akhenaten put the Aten above all gods and built a new capital, Akhetaten (Amarna). A new religion needed new images: the god was the visible disk, and the royal family was shown as the link between the Aten and everyone else. Scholars offer several readings of the strange bodies: a religious statement (the king as unique, perhaps as both father and mother of his people), a deliberate court fashion, or a mix. A medical explanation has been suggested, but it has not been confirmed. There is no agreement.

The most famous Amarna work is the painted bust of Queen Nefertiti, found in 1912 in the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose and now in Berlin. Its calm beauty shows that the style softened over time. After Akhenaten, under Tutankhamun and later kings, art returned to the older rules, keeping some of the softness.

blocks.title: Which era?
blocks.q: A relief shows a king and queen kissing their daughters under a sun disk whose rays end in hands. When is it from?
steps: Rays ending in hands: the Aten.
Intimate family scenes were new at Amarna.
So it is from Akhenaten’s reign.
blocks.a: The Amarna age.

blocks.title: Evidence of illness?
blocks.q: A website says Akhenaten’s statues prove he had a disease. How should you answer?
steps: The statues follow a new artistic style.
A medical cause has not been confirmed.
Scholars debate what the style meant.
blocks.a: They show a style, whose meaning is debated, not proof of illness.

blocks.html: Taking Amarna portraits as medical evidence of illness. They reflect a new artistic style; what it meant is debated. Quick check: other members of the court are shown the same way.

blocks.html: Most of this course has been about temples, kings and tombs. But as Many Gods, Many Forms showed, Egypt had gods for every need, and some of the most loved belonged to the home.
At home, people turned to protectors like Bes and Taweret, especially for childbirth and children.

head: God
Looks
Protects
rows: a dwarf with a lion-like face, often sticking out his tongue, with a feathered crown
a standing hippopotamus with a lion’s paws and a crocodile’s tail
a cow or a woman with cow horns
blocks.cap: Gods of the household.

blocks.html: Childbirth and early childhood were the most dangerous times of life, and families wanted every protection they could get. Bes and Taweret were fierce on purpose: their frightening faces looked outward at whatever might threaten the family. That is why Bes appears on beds, headrests, mirrors and cosmetic jars, the objects near a person in the most unguarded moments, and why Taweret amulets were worn by women expecting a child.

items: Houses at the workmen’s village of Deir el-Medina had wall niches and small shrines for images of gods and of honored ancestors.
In the Middle Kingdom, curved wands of hippopotamus ivory carved with protective creatures were used to guard mothers and babies.
Families kept amulets, small statues and painted images of the gods they relied on most.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: pr, "house": the plan of a house with its door. Household gods guarded the pr.

blocks.title: Who is it?
blocks.q: A wooden headrest is carved with a dwarf-like god with a lion’s face and his tongue out. Who is he, and why is he there?
steps: A dwarf with a lion-like face is Bes.
He protected sleepers from harm in the night.
So he appears on a headrest.
blocks.a: Bes, guarding the sleeper.

blocks.title: Choosing a protector
blocks.q: A woman expecting a child wanted a protective amulet. Which goddess would she most likely choose?
steps: Taweret, the hippopotamus goddess, protected women in childbirth.
Her amulets were common.
blocks.a: Taweret.

blocks.html: Thinking only temple gods mattered. Daily life had its own gods, and ordinary people relied on them. Quick check: look at what is carved on everyday objects like beds and mirrors.
Household protection, as in Household Gods, was often worn on the body. Amulets were small objects of faience, stone or metal that carried a protective sign.
People wore amulets for protection, in life and in the tomb: the wedjat eye, the scarab, the ankh, the djed pillar and the tyet knot.

head: Amulet
Meaning
rows: the healed eye of Horus: wholeness and protection
Khepri, the rising sun: renewal (ḫpr, "come into being")
stability; linked with the backbone of Osiris (ḏd)
the "knot of Isis", often of red stone: her protection
blocks.cap: Five common amulets.

blocks.html: Many amulets are hieroglyphs that could be worn. A sign meant what it showed, and Egyptians believed signs could act, as tomb scenes did. Wearing the ankh carried "life"; wearing the djed carried "stability". Myth gave others their power: the wedjat recalls the eye of Horus, torn out by Seth and made whole again, so it brought healing and wholeness. Amulets were placed among a mummy’s wrappings too; the large heart scarab, set over the heart, carried spell 30B of the Book of the Dead.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ꜥnḫ, "life": the ankh sign, with n and ḫ as phonetic complements. Worn alone, the sign was an amulet.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: ḫpr, "come into being": the scarab sign, linked with Khepri and renewal.

blocks.html: Most amulets were made of faience, a glazed material that could be shaped in molds and came out blue or green, the colors of life. Richer people had them in gold, carnelian or lapis lazuli. The Book of the Dead even names the right material for some: spell 155 is for a djed of gold, spell 156 for a tyet of red jasper.

blocks.title: Reading an amulet
blocks.q: A small faience pillar with four horizontal bands at the top is found in a burial. What is it, and what did it give?
steps: A pillar with bands at the top is the djed.
It meant stability and was linked with Osiris’s backbone.
blocks.a: A djed amulet, for stability.

blocks.title: Why a beetle?
blocks.q: Why would anyone wear a beetle?
steps: The scarab’s name, ḫpr, means "come into being".
Egyptians linked it with Khepri, the sun rising each morning.
So it stood for renewal.
blocks.a: It stood for renewal, like the rising sun.

blocks.html: Thinking amulets were only jewelry. They could be beautiful, but they were worn for protection, in life and in the tomb. Quick check: ask what sign the amulet carries and what that sign means.

blocks.html: Temples were closed to most people, as Cult Temples and Memorial Temples explained. Yet ordinary Egyptians did reach the gods and their own dead. Oracles and letters to the dead, which build on the offering cult at the tomb, show how.
People asked gods questions through oracles at festivals, and wrote letters to dead relatives asking for help.

Especially from the New Kingdom on, a god could answer questions when its boat-shrine came out in procession. A question was put to the god, aloud or written on a potsherd. The priests carrying the boat felt it move: forward could mean yes, backward no, or the boat could stop before one of several written answers. People asked about lost property, disputes, illness and choices. At Deir el-Medina, the workmen consulted the deified king Amenhotep I, honored as their village’s founder, and many of their questions survive on ostraca.

The dead were still part of the family and could act among the living. Some people wrote letters to dead parents or spouses, often on a bowl that held a food offering left at the tomb. The letters ask for help (with an illness, a quarrel, a hope for a child) or ask the dead to stop troubles the writer blamed on them. Examples are known from the Old Kingdom on.

Both practices rest on beliefs from earlier lessons. A god dwelt in its image, so when the image came out, the god could be asked. The dead lived on, needed offerings and could hear, so a letter left with food would reach them. Small "ear stelae", carved with ears, asked a god to listen to a prayer. Together they show that religion was part of daily life, not only of temples and kings.

blocks.name: eg-glyphs
blocks.cap: sḏm, "hear": the cow’s ear, with s and m. People asked the gods, and the dead, to hear them.

blocks.title: How did the god answer?
blocks.q: At a festival, a farmer asks Amun whether his neighbor took his goat. How might the answer come?
steps: The god’s boat is carried by priests in the procession.
The boat moves forward for yes or back for no.
The answer is the god’s judgment.
blocks.a: By the movement of the god’s boat.

blocks.title: Reading a bowl
blocks.q: A pottery bowl from a tomb has writing on it addressed to a dead mother, asking her to help her son. What is it?
steps: It is addressed to a dead relative.
It was left at the tomb, likely with food.
blocks.a: A letter to the dead.

blocks.html: Thinking ordinary people had no way to reach the gods. Oracles, prayers, ear stelae and letters to the dead show how they did. Quick check: look for the questions on ostraca and the letters on bowls.
